Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure to present two petitions, signed by over 1,100 people in my riding of Carleton- Gloucester and surrounding areas.

These petitioners are as outraged as I am that the serial killer board game, with the object of having players kill as many babies as possible, is allowed to be distributed and sold in Canada.
They call for an immediate ban of this board game and any other material which advocate violence.

I have the honour to support them in this. I congratulate all the petitioners who took part and I ask the government to act on this issue as quickly as possible.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to present a petition on behalf of a number of teachers from central British Columbia, adding to what would be many hundreds of petitioners.

Routine Proceedings
They point out that under the Income Tax Act selected professional groups can deduct or write off dues, equipment or services necessary for the operation of their profession.
They indicate that teachers are precluded from receiving such benefits. They ask the Government of Canada to introduce legislation that would provide equal treatment by amendment to the Income Tkx Act so that teachers would be treated in the same way as other professionals.
Madam Speaker, on another matter the petitioners are by and large from the Kamloops area. They point out their opposition to any possibility of water diversion to the United States.

Madam Speaker, I would like to table a petition from Amos, Saint-Felix-de-Dalquier, Saint-Mathieu, Saint-Dominique-du-Ros-aire and Preissac in Abitibi. The petitioners say that violent movies on television are dangerous and therefore unacceptable because they incite more violence.
They mention that all toys that incite violent games are unacceptable and should not be made. They also state that freedom of the press should be limited in reporting acts of violence.
Therefore the petitioners humbly ask Parliament to legislate on the above-mentioned points in order to eliminate violence in our society, so as to better protect our children and give all our fellow citizens a better quality of life.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present this morning, both dealing with the same matter.

With respect to resolution No. 1992-44 adopted by the United

the rights of indigenous peoples, (a) what comments has the
government given to (i) the Working Group of Indigenous Populations
Routine Proceedings
of the Subcommission on Prevention of Discrimination and Protection of Minorities (ii) the Secretary General concerning the draft universal declaration on the rights of indigenous peoples (b) has the government made a financial contribution to the United Nations Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples and, if so, in what amount (c) what steps has the government taken or does it intend-to take to ensure the full participation of indigenous organizations within Canada to participate in the activities related to the tasks of the Working Group of Indigenous Populations (d) has the government provided funding to send delegates to the Indigenous Youth Conference to be held in July 1992 in Quebec City?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Working Group of Indigenous Populations (WGIP) has been engaged for the last 10 years in considering standards unique to the rights of indigenous populations. Representatives of indigenous groups have been putting their case to the five experts of the WGIP. These experts, drawing from their legal and human rights background, the experience of indigenous people and the observations of governments, have produced a draft declaration on the rights of indigenous people.
The Government of Canada has played an active and participatory role in the activities of the WGIP. It has the lead in drafting the resolution in the Commission of Human Rights from which the WGIP draws its mandate. The government has also contributed on a regular basis to the indigenous voluntary fund of the human rights centre to enable indigenous representatives from the Third World to attend and participate in the WGIP sessions. These contributions are important for those indigenous groups which do not have the financial means to attend the sessions or those whose attendance is not sanctioned by their governments. Rigoberta Menchu, this year's winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, has benefited from this fund, financed as well by the Nordic countries, the Netherlands, Australia and New Zealand.
The most important contribution of Canada has been the sharing of its experience with the WGIP and other governments attending the sessions. Probably no other country has been as involved in the settling of claims of lands, grievances from the past or in looking to new concepts of governance within the state. Canada is seen by other governments and indeed many indigenous groups as a leader. This is but one of the reasons why Canada has been given the honour and the responsibility of the lead on UN resolutions regarding indigenous people.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
The Cree youth of James Bay received active support from the government for the holding of their Indigenous Youth Conference. The delegation of Canada at the Human Rights Commission ensured that the 1991 mandate resolution for the WGIP included a reference to the conference to encourage others to attend. The Department of External Affairs used its network to spread news of the conference through our embassies and to facilitate the travel arrangements from countries requiring visas to enter Canada.
The department also encouraged the authorities of the Government of Quebec to support the conference with funds and logistics. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Canadian International Development Agency each contributed $125,000 for the over-all logistics of the conference and to enable indigenous youth from around the world to attend. By all accounts the conference was a success and brought much credit to the aboriginal youth of Canada and the Cree nation in particular.

speechtext: The hon. member for Bona-vista-Trinity-Conception.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased and somewhat overwhelmed by the support from my colleagues this morning, particularly the House leader and the Whip. I am delighted that I am starting off this very busy day with support from this side of the House, from my two highly esteemed and very important colleagues. I even got a sort of welcome from the other side of the House. I see even the NDP is smiling. I hope they are all smiling and clapping their hands when my presentation is completed.
This borrowing bill is a very important bill. I know the government will try to get this through as quickly as possible. It will try to limit debate on it so that Canadians will not be too aware of how it is running the economy and how the finances of this country have been put together.
In order to put it in perspective I have to go back the four and a half years I have been in this House, but I also want to reflect back to 1984. It is my understanding that the three essential elements of any government are to legislate, to legitimate and to educate.
As far as legislation is concerned, the government has a good record in numbers of bills put through the House, the numbers of projets de loi passed. The quality and the legitimacy of the legislation along with the education process certainly causes me, and a lot of members of this House on both sides perhaps and the Canadian public,
February 11, 1993

difficulty. I believe this confusion of the three principles is one of the root causes of our problems as politicians.
I have only to speak of the unemployment insurance bill, Bill C-21. The goods and services tax bill will go down in history as a bad piece of legislation introduced at the wrong time and in the wrong manner. I include the bill on Canada Post, the bill reducing VIA Rail, the bill reducing transfer payments to the provinces.
The most recent bill we have been discussing which will have difficulty getting through the House-the government is bound to limit debate-is on the drastic and insensitive cuts to unemployment insurance. It is the subject of major discussion in our country.
Countless bills have been the subject of great discussion in this House and regrettably the opposition was not given the time or the volume of effort necessary to oppose the bills and to discuss them to the point consensus could be reached.
I believe I am safe in sayin I am not going to quote statistics, as I have done a dozen times in this House, and as my colleagues have also that the record number of closures and debate limitations that have been placed on the House of Commons by this government is greater than all the other numbers of those combined since Confederation. In other words, debate has been limited more in the last eight and a half years than it has been at any other time up to and including 1984 since Confederation.
The legislation part I have discussed and I will now turn to legitimacy. In a democracy, how really legitimate in a generic sense, not in the legal sense, is a bill or are a number of measures that are passed in Parliament, the highest court in the land, when back in the previous 125 years of Confederation, the limiting of debate, or closure on a debate was almost enough to call a general election.
It has happened so often in this Parliament and in the Parliament before that it is now common procedure and hardly gets a note in the media. I will leave it to hon. members to decide how to combine the legitimacy with the legislative aspect.
As for the education part, I believe Canadians are confused on what it is this government is doing. I can quote countless examples of statements that have been made or election promises that have been declared. The
Government Orders
Prime Minister has said certain matters were sacred trusts, or these are our plans, or this is what we want to do in the election. However, as the legislation unfolds and as the mood of the government becomes apparent, it is obvious to the House, to the media, and indeed to Canadians in a downstream manner that the promises made were not kept and the sacred trusts that were discussed were thrown out the window. It is an indication of what happened in 1984, but more so in 1988, that if it was not diametrically opposed to what in fact happened, it certainly did not follow the course of the promise.
I will use two examples. I will use the example of the sacred trust to which the Prime Minister referred, the unemployment insurance program. In October 1988 during the campaign he said, and it was repeated by the minister responsible for Newfoundland, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, that he reiterated and reinforced that unemployment insurance and social programs were sacred trusts.
A sacred trust is a very strong term. The Concise Oxford Dictionary describes sacred as associated with or dedicated to God and trust is defined as a firm belief in the reliability or truth or strength of a person or thing. The words sacred trust convey a commitment. The Prime Minister did not just casually mention to Canadians that he would maintain a social program, or he would do this or he would do that. It was presented to Canadians as a commitment of a higher order and as a pledge that was related to God.
Having pledged that the unemployment insurance program and the social programs were a sacred trust and nothing would happen to them, even as the election was being planned and the campaign unfolded, officials were preparing legislation which eventually became Bill C-21. It totally changed the unemployment insurance system and in fact took the government out of the business. It increased the input from the employers and the employees by over 50 per cent and took away job development programs which in Atlantic Canada have been the mainstay of job creation. Regrettably but pragmatically it was a very important thing.
I recall when this happened in June three years ago. I am still explaining to people why jobs that were planned and why projects that were planned were, at the stroke of a pen, taken away. I had no control over it. The officials in Atlantic Canada had no control over it. The

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
government just wiped its face and got on to the next unpopular legislation.
Another sacred trust, although it was not put forward as a sacred trust, was regional development. On October 3, 1988 in Saint John, New Brunswick, during the election campaign the Prime Minister said-I do not have the exact words here-words to the effect that "I am not going to govern a country where all regions are not treated equally".
That statement was made in October and in the budget that came out in the spring of 1989-1 think it was April 27, one day premature because of some difficulties the government experienced-the Western Diversification Fund for the prairie provinces was reduced by $55 million, and in my case ACOA was reprofiled to lose 25 per cent of the funds and resources that were so important for regional development. There is another promise that not only was changed by some minor significance, it was a total change from what was promised.
There are other areas that I want to examine, and I hope that time will permit. I mentioned unemployment insurance and I talked about regional development and funds committed to regional development. While I am on that subject I want to mention transfer payments.
Transfer payments to the extremities of Canada are very important. Very briefly, in Newfoundland where the budget is between $3 and $3.5 billion it used to be that 49 per cent of that resource input came from the federal government. When 49 to 50 per cent of all the expenditures of one province come from the federal government it is easily understood that if you tampering with that input of $1.5 billion plus in any way is going to cause major perturbation, major upsets in the finances of a government.
In the case of Newfoundland, starting in 1989 with the reduction in the growth of transfer payments, the input to Newfoundland was reduced from 49 per cent to 45 per cent. This represents a total input of $200 million. This has meant downstream that the provincial government-
I would say it has done it quietly and without major complaint-has got on with the job of running the province. It has had to cut back in critical areas, particularly welfare but in the general sense not necessarily on the social programs which have increased because of
this. It has had to cut back on education and health care. Those are critical areas that were directly related to transfer payments.
Newfoundland is not alone. Atlantic Canada is not alone. With the implementation of Bill C-20 which capped the transfer payments by the year 2000 the federal government will be denying Canadians $97.6 billion, almost $100 billion of services and resources, particularly those focused on health care and post-secondary institutions. That is a major blow to Newfoundland. It is a major blow to Atlantic Canada and the rest of Canada.
On the question of transfer payments in health, education and particularly social programs there is a group of parliamentarians on the other side of the House, a group of wealthy business concerns in Canada and a group of people who really have not given this much thought who are beginning, because it is trendy, to say that we can no longer afford the social programs Canadians have become accustomed to.
The deficit we have this year is the deficit we had eight and a half years ago. I am not going to get into that because I have spoken on that twice already in the last 10 days. With the rising cost of social programs and the need to do all the other things this government has been trying to do we can no longer really afford social programs.
A closer examination and a better analysis of that trendy thought does not bear evidence. It does not bear out the facts. The facts are that Canada's social spending as I speak is 21.5 per cent of our gross domestic product. The average for all the other industrialized countries in the OECD is 25.6 per cent. So do not give me false information or try to mislead me with the hogwash information that we cannot afford our social programs.
Many of the European countries that have high standards of living and successful economies spend even a larger percentage of their GDP on social programs: Belgium, 37.6 per cent; Holland, 36.1 per cent; West Germany, one of the best industrialized countries in the world, 31.5 per cent; France, 29 per cent. The only major industrialized countries where social spending is lower than Canada are the United States at 20.8 per cent, and
February 11, 1993

we are trying to emulate them with the free trade agreement and the NAFTA, and Japan at 17.5 per cent.
In my mind, borne out by the facts, clearly the portrait of Canadian social programs is very much in a favourable position with the other industrialized countries of the world that we compare with in the G-7 analysis and that we compete with.
Therefore, I do not want to hear much more of this trendy thought that we cannot afford social programs. Their name of the game is that we have to hit the social business, we have to reduce transfer payments because we cannot find money any other way.
In November I had the opportunity and the privilege to sit in on the closed session with the Auditor General and later the open public session. In the Auditor General's report the charge and observation was made that hundreds of millions of dollars were being lost in tax revenue because of the way we organized our corporate tax and to a certain extent our income tax for offshore capture. Some of my colleagues may recall, I believe it was on November 24 or 25, 1992 during Question Period, that question was put to the Minister of Finance and he denied it.
After meetings with the public accounts committee and other questions that were asked the finance department officials finally admitted that hundreds of millions of dollars in corporate tax revenues were lost to offshore tax schemes as the Auditor General claimed. This did not occur until some time in December, I believe. That was certainly a reversal of the department's initial stand. Not only does it know that it can get taxes and incomes from other revenue sources but it also denies that this possibility is there.
Back to the three principles of government in a democracy of legislating, legitimizing and educating. That is a very poor way to educate those desperate Canadians who are wondering legitimately and with great motivation how we can reduce the national debt and the deficit.
I now want to talk about another area that is of current and topical concern in the House of Commons and in Parliament. This is unemployment insurance.
The present bill before the House is one that will change yet again unemployment insurance principles
Government Orders
which were developed by the Liberal Party in the early 1940s. It will change unemployment insurance to the point where its effectiveness will be reduced another notch.
Unemployment is at a record high and is predicted to be by the Conference Board of Canada the second highest in the G-7 countries at 11.3 per cent for this year. Instead of attacking this difficulty and organizing programs to put Canadians back to work the budget announcement in early December penalized the unemployed to the point of $2.5 billion. They are already paying 50 per cent more in unemployment insurance fees. Now the government wants to reduce the benefit rate on the maximum insurable weekly earnings of $745 from 60 per cent to 57 per cent. It also wants to eliminate benefits to workers who quit without just cause or are fired for misconduct.
I heard this morning that those unfortunate people who through no fault of their own and in a lot of cases through no fault of their companies are being retired and receive severance will be cut off from unemployment insurance.
There are other areas I could mention in wrapping up. Canada Post is an area of major concern with 10,000 jobs being lost. Another area is our social programs.
In conclusion, if the government had put measures in place that would have increased growth and employment it would not have had to borrow as much. People would be paying more taxes, would be showing more confidence in the government and the country. If the government added this to those areas of corporate taxes and offshore taxes it is not capturing worth hundreds of millions of dollars, then we would not be in the predicament we are. I do not see any change between now and the next election. The government will have to answer to the people after this bill is passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I always listen with great care when my hon. friend from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception speaks. I have two questions I would like to ask.
I must observe first that there is clearly a difference of philosophy on his side of the House compared with those of us over here. Those of us over here think that if revenues are down expenditures should be brought in line rather than just carrying on and ignoring the fact

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
that perhaps there is not the same amount of money to work with.
The government's revenues are down some $8 billion this year. Obviously that means if we are going to spend at the same level, let alone increase expenditures, we are going to lose control of the deficit completely.
I have noticed his leader is proposing to scrap the GST. This is now definitive we are told. He had said earlier he would scrap it, then he said he would keep it, then he said he would modify it and now he is going to scrap it. I am not sure what he is going to replace it with because that has not been made clear. If the $15 billion or $16 billion of revenue that accrues is added to the $8 billion shortfall then $23 billion or $24 billion has to be made up.
What is the hon. member's proposal to replace the GST? Is it going to be the new GST, the Grit sneaky tax as it is being called, which is apparently being proposed? That would be a hidden tax, the business transfer tax, which would be on everything including food, medical services, and so on.
Where does he propose to make up the revenue shortfall in order to provide the programs that certainly we on this side of the House would agree are desirable?
My second question has to do with the EH-101 contract. His leader has said that one of the ways to make up for the deficit shortfall is to cancel the EH-101 contract which will cost $4.4 billion over 20 years. That is not really a big thing on a year-to-year basis in that sense. They sometimes forget it is spread over 20 years.
I know that many of his former colleagues in the navy starting I might say with Admiral John Anderson, the new chief of defence staff and the new deputy chief, also an admiral in the navy, are all very ardently in support of the necessity of the EH-101s, both for search and rescue purposes but also for maintaining the preparedness of our military.
Does he agree with his leader that the EH-101 contract should be scrapped or does he think this government is right to proceed with it? If he believes it should be scrapped, what is his proposed alternative? Does he think we should also scrap the Canadian patrol
frigates which without those helicopters cannot obviously fulfil the purpose for which they were established? I put those questions to my hon. friend and I look forward to his answers.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to hear from my good friend the hon. member for South Shore. I am very familiar with that part of the country and love it dearly. It is a lovely part of Nova Scotia.
Quite frankly sometimes I am sorry he is in the position of having to argue some of the cases that he does. I know he has difficulties with his constituents in following these policies and that is the unfortunate fallout of politics. It happens to all of us from time to time.
I remind my hon. colleague it is the government that is on the firing line for having introduced the GST, the most unpopular tax in the history of this country, possibly in the history of the world. There was the misinformation that it was going to be revenue neutral at a time when we were heading into one of the worst depressions ever experienced in this country. If he thinks he is going to put the ball in my court when this government is responsible for these three aspects, he is wrong. He asked me what we were going to do about the GST.
The last figure I could get showed that the GST accounts for 12 per cent of the government's total income of $122.2 billion in the last fiscal year. That hits those in the middle class more than anyone else because the middle class and the lower income class spend more of their money on essentials that are taxed with the goods and services tax. While the tax was supposed to be spread across a reasonable distribution it hits middle and low income people harder, irrespective of the credits. Also last week we heard that small businesses are going under at a record high of 77,000. So do not blame me for the GST. He is asking me what we are going to do.
The Auditor General's report says that the goods and services tax accounted for around $29.5 billion and the government says that it accounted for $15 billion-we are not sure whether that was the $1.5 billion it cost to collect. How does anybody on that side of the House have the gall and audacity to ask this side of the House, given that the figure could be $30 billion or $15 billion, how we are going to introduce a tax to replace the revenues collected from the GST?
February 11, 1993

We will not continue with the GST in its present form. We will not continue to tax the kind of people who have been taxed by the GST. We will not continue the onerous burden that small businesses have had to bear to the point where they are going out of business. I know many and I am sure my colleague from South Shore knows many.
He wants to talk about the helicopter and I am quite happy to talk about the helicopter. If he were here in the House when I made a presentation last Thursday, and maybe he has read my presentation, he would know why we have a problem with the EH-101 helicopter. Our position is very clear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is not a problem with that side of the House. It's a problem with the front row.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my colleague asked a question. If he wants an answer he has to listen for it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We're not getting an answer.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
They are getting an answer but the Minister of the Environment says they are not getting an answer. He would hear it if he would listen instead of shouting and screaming and trying to pressure people into doing things they really do not want to do. I would not accuse this side of the House of doing that because they are all very well disciplined. I know that the three gentlemen in front of me are very reasonable and want to listen to what I have to say.
The position of our leader and the position of the Liberal Party on July 24 was no different from what it is now. We believe that something must change with regard to the Sea King helicopter and the search and rescue fleets. They need refurbishing. They need to be re* placed. That is on record.
However at a time when there are 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, when the number of soup kitchens is at a record high, when the unemployment line-ups are great, when the debt is mushrooming, and when small businesses are going broke at a record rate we question the government's priorities in committing $4.5 billion to helicopters.
Subsequent to that position, in July the Auditor General examined the defence management system that handles these megaprojects and said it was ineffective and expensive. He may be wrong, but if he is wrong I want the minister to tell the House. I have given the Minister of National Defence, two different ones, two
Government Orders
opportunities to say that our system is great and explain why it is great. The government will not discuss it in Parliament. It will not discuss it in defence committee. It will not discuss it anywhere. The minister should say whether it is wrong or right. The Canadian people have been told that $4.5 billion of taxpayers' money is being committed to a system that the Auditor General in his report to Canadians says is ineffective and expensive.
In January the Minister of National Defence herself said that she was not convinced that this was the right program. Do not point the finger at my leader, do not point the finger at this side of the House and ask why we are doing it because the minister herself has done it.
When she is not convinced, being privileged to the discussion in cabinet and on the expenditure committee, how in the name of everything holy can she expect us to be totally convinced? How can she expect the opposition to roll over and play dead on $4.5 billion? This is one of the biggest programs in terms of spending in Canadian history. It is one-half of the total cost of the frigate program, which I would remind my hon. friend was a Liberal program. We are totally dedicated to that and we will continue to be dedicated to that. Why we are opposing it is pretty obvious.
If the member for South Shore thinks that I am going to bolt my caucus because he thinks I do not agree with my leader he is wrong because it is only the other side of the House that does that. It has lost more members than I have fingers and toes. It is not going to happen with this party and it is not going to happen on this side of the House because I support my leader and I support his decisions for the reasons I have given.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am really quite pleased to follow in the footsteps of my colleague in speaking to this borrowing bill. One of the things that the people of Canada would like to know is when the government is going to call an election.
The government has made such a mess of things and is continuing to make a mess of things.
They really want to know when it is going to call an election. It is really frustrating. I am just wondering when the government can answer that question because everyone in Canada is waiting with baited breath. They think that maybe they will be able to get an alternative that can actually consult people, speak to them, try not to hurt them, and above all not always introduce the wrong thing at the wrong time.
One of the key questions is when there will be a budget. Normally the government presents a budget at the end of February but this time it is saying just think back to the economic statement and do not worry about the budget. The government is going to wait until Bill Clinton presents his budget. Then it will tell us what it is doing.
What kind of an answer is that? Come on. Either give us a budget or call an election and let us get on with governing this country. There are too many problems to be addressed. This is a tired, old, and paralyzed government. The members opposite are all waiting to see whether the Prime Minister will step down. That is really what is on everybody's minds.
February 11, 1993	COMMONS
There are people running all over the place and not really getting anything done. Everyone is waiting. It is especially important that the Prime Minister make up his mind, put the question to rest once and for all and step down and then we can go on with encouraging others in their leadership campaigns. Then we can possibly get to the real business of governing a country and addressing the economy.
We talked about the economy and how this Conservative government had promised that after the referendum in October it would address the economy. I am very disappointed with the way it has addressed the economy.
The government has given us a drug bill that was more like a price hike for the average Canadian. It will cause very serious harm to the medicare system in this country. It has given us a bailout of the airline industry that was a lot more like a crash than anything else. Our airline industry continues to be in desperate shape.
The government has promised us jobs but the only jobs that we have seen are cushy seats for this government's friends. That is not what the people of Canada mean when they talk about jobs. It is now giving us a UI bill that it claims will catch all these bad Canadians who really do not want to work but want to sit at home and collect unemployment insurance.
I remind those members how difficult it is right now to get a job for most Canadians. Furthermore, if they have a job they do not leave it because collecting unemployment insurance is not the panacea that the government seems to think it is. Right now there are very serious penalties for people who leave jobs with no valid reason, as there should be, but they are not in the majority.
The government must address the problems that these people face: the shutdowns and layoffs that cause these people to not have a job in the first place and that causes there to be no other jobs for them to find.
I feel certain that after the next election many members on the other side of the House will face that and realize that it is not easy out there to get a job. There are young people with good educations but there are very few jobs for them. They are working part time as sales clerks and so on even though they may have a Masters degree in business administration or degrees in economics. This is a reality that we all must face. It is a serious

Government Orders
problem. We cannot just sit by and wait for things to happen.
This government speaks of its strategy toward the economy. Its short-term strategy is to do nothing, hope the U.S. does something and ride on its coat-tails.
Its medium term strategy is to pretend it is doing something good because then it will not have to worry about it. Things will get better and the government members can pretend it was because of them.
Then there is the long-term strategy to just keep going because it probably will not be there to bear the consequences. It can pass the problem on to the next group. That is no strategy.
We have to face what we have today. We have to stop being so partisan. I am saying this as I stand here in the opposition and perhaps at times I am as guilty as the others. We have to stop fighting one another. We have to start co-operating. I am not just talking about the federal level, I am talking about all levels of government.
For instance, this year we are going to top the $450 billion mark in the national debt. That is just at the federal level. We are not taking into consideration at this point the debts at the provincial level and the problems that all of these serious constraints cause to the other levels of government such as school boards and municipal systems.
We have to stop shifting the blame, playing little games among ourselves and saying we are going to cut back on transfer payments. Then the provinces will blame the federal government members and we will say: "It is their problem. It is not ours". Then the provinces will cut back on transfers to municipalities and the story goes on.
We all must realize that if a province has a debt it is also a national debt. If the federal government gets out of debt at the expense of an ever increasing debt at the provincial level, we are not going to be any better off. We are going to be worse off. It is long overdue for the federal government to sit down with the provincial governments and decide how they are going to proceed in the future. They must stop fighting one another.
We have an example of that happening now. There has been an announcement of cutbacks in grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities. Municipalities have nowhere to go. They are at the bottom of the line. If there is a

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
cutback in the grants this government gives municipalities in lieu of paying municipal taxes then it is the municipal taxpayer who picks up the burden. The same taxpayer is paying income tax to the federal government and the provinces.
Is there not a better way to distribute the burden more equitably? It will not be easy, but it is absolutely essential. We all know that the debt is a serious concern. The sooner we distribute the burden more equitably the better off we will be as a country.
We have some very good things going for us. If we can build on them we will move ahead far more quickly than in this partisan atmosphere where we always blame somebody else for our misfortunes. We are all Canadians and we are all responsible.
I know we have talked about many things with regard to debt, deficit and the GST. I want to remind the people in this House that according to figures presented to the public accounts committee the GST burdened the Canadian public to the tune of $29.5 billion. That is not the net figure. It is what was actually taken into government coffers before expenses. It means that for every dollar of GST collected it cost 50 cents in 1991-92. That is not a very efficient tax.
There is a lot of confusion in terms of the information given to MPs about the GST in that particular year. I am aware that both the Auditor General and the Comptroller General were asked to clarify the differences between the $29.5 billion and the $15 billion net result of the tax. Neither of them has really been able to answer the questions. We are awaiting responses.
How can we opposition members give the government members all the answers when they cannot answer our questions? What is the real effect of the GST? Who is being hurt? Who is paying? Let us know that. It is absolutely essential that the people of Canada be given the whole truth and nothing but the truth on this tax.
I know for a fact that a tax bill was introduced yesterday by a Ways and Means motion. Now a tax bill of this kind will have a lot of measures and means but it also includes a section that would remove the GST from access to information. Why would they remove the GST from access to information? It is quite normal to want to protect corporations from revealing their sales figures, et cetera, much as you protect people by not giving out information on their private tax returns. I respect that, but I am really worried that it will be a way for this government to restrict information to the opposition and
the people of Canada about what exactly has happened with the GST.
I would like the government to answer that question for me, because so far there has been no answer. This is very serious and we want to know. If we are prevented from accessing the information how can we give realistic answers? Our questions must be answered. We have to stop playing games. We need to know the facts.
The Comptroller General and the Auditor General are having a difficult time answering questions. When there are secrets being kept it does not look good. Where there is smoke there is usually also fire. That is what this looks like to me. I ask the government to be absolutely above reproach in terms of access to information and stop playing games.
When it comes to prospects for this country I know that the majority of Canadians are hard workers and do not want to be on unemployment insurance. There will always be people who are not quite as honest as they should be, but the majority of Canadians are honest, hard-working people. When they do claim unemployment insurance they are very much aware of how serious it is.
I think sometimes the people of Canada are not aware of how serious the penalties are if they make a mistake and how they can be charged $100 or $200. For instance, if they make a mistake reporting income on their UI claim form and worked a few hours in one week, they will not only have to pay back the $100 they forgot to mention, but they might be fined as much as $100 or $200 for that one mistake. There are very strict guidelines, as there should be. But let us not pretend that all people on UI would cheat the system because they would not. I know many people who are very frightened of making a mistake.
I also know people who have not really made a mistake but have been seriously penalized by the UIC. I know of a recent case of a man who was laid off when his company closed down. He is a family man with three young children and a wife at home. He had worked for the same company for 16.5 years and was given a severance package that was the equivalent of approximately six months of wages. In case members do not know, when a person gets a severance package he or she is not allowed to claim UI until he or she has exhausted that severance package. In other words, he would have had to wait six months and if he did not have a job at that time then he could have applied for unemployment

insurance. This is fine because it at least gave him a chance in those six months to find a job.
This man really looked for a job in those six months. He was able to find some part-time, minimum wage occupation for eight weeks of that time but was laid off. He took a short-term job because he is very conscientious, did not want to be a burden on anyone and wanted to support his own family. At the end of his severance package when his money was gone and he still did not have a job, not even a part-time job which he was willing to take if he could find one, he applied for unemployment insurance.
Because he had worked those eight weeks at a minimum wage job the money he will now receive is far lower than what he would have received had he not worked those eight weeks at a minimum wage job. This man has been penalized because his remittances to UI from this minimum wage job were far reduced from what he was making before.
I want the Canadian people to know that the UI system is a very harsh system now. It is not easy to take advantage of. It always surprises me when I hear what people go through.
For instance, two people worked as cooks in a restaurant. They left because they could not take any more abuse from the owner of the restaurant. They both left at the same time, applied for UI and were fined for having quit their jobs. Not only were they fined 10 weeks in the case of one and 9 weeks in the case of the other-and do not ask me why there was a difference because I do not know-but they only received 50 per cent of what they would have received otherwise.
This case has gone before arbitration and has not been settled yet. They may get full benefits at some point and they may have some portion of the penalty reinstated, but it has been at least eight months since they left their abusive employer. They have not received that money yet and they may never get it.

I want the people of Canada to realize that these are the kinds of measures in place today. They should not be side-tracked by this government that insists on bringing in the wrong measures at the wrong time. I ask the government to do the right thing for once. Let us give this country a chance and call an election, please.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has certainly been an enlightening debate so far. I am pleased to participate in it.
The bill before us is Bill C-98, the borrowing bill by which the government is trying to get authorization from the House of Commons to borrow another $34.4 billion.
Before I get into my remarks regarding the bill, in case there are any friends and relatives watching us on television today, I would like to explain that while I realize my face has never been my number one asset in politics it is looking a little worse than usual. It is not as a result of political persecution from the other side but because of a close encounter with the ground when I was tobogganing with my son on Sunday. It is my favourite winter sport, never having been a figure skater like my hon. colleague across the way.
That aside, I would like to deal with the challenge that is before us. If we do not like the way the government is spending money, borrowing money and handling the nation's finances, what are the alternatives?
In my remarks I would certainly like to deal with all the national issues that are involved but it is much easier to focus on my own constituency of Prince Albert- Churchill River. It is a very diverse constituency; 46 per cent is the city of Prince Albert, 36 per cent northern and aboriginal population and 22 per cent rural. In many ways it is a microcosm of the country.
The reason I would like to focus on my constituency is because I do not believe we need to be borrowing as much as we are today. I believe there are better ways of spending our money. I would like to demonstrate that by using my constituency as an example.
I was first elected in 1988. When I was running for election the question was already before us: How are you going to pay for the alternatives that you are suggesting? I took up that challenge and did some research. I found that in 1988, four and one-half years ago, the federal government alone was spending $125 million in that constituency on unemployment insurance and welfare.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
Those high welfare costs are a result of the fact that 25 per cent of that population are treaty Indian people. The welfare costs are paid directly by the government. Unfortunately 80 per cent of that population is unemployed. Also there is the federal government's contribution to cost sharing arrangements with the province.
We started in 1988 with $125 million. I have kept track of that over the years. With this new financial statement going into this new budget year I find the federal government is spending $170 million in my constituency alone on welfare and unemployment insurance.
If there is any waste of money, it is that particular sum of money. Not only is it costing the taxpayers directly in having to shell out that amount of money, but there are also the secondary costs that come with the broken lives that need to be repaired health costs and the cost of imprisonment of people and all costs associated with that level of poverty and with those people in the constituency who are not working.
How does this government propose to tackle this problem of the deficit, in other words, spending more money than we are taking in? The government is planning to cut UI. In a constituency like mine where 80 per cent of the people are unemployed the 3 per cent cut in UI benefits will really be a disaster for people, and not only in economic terms. In a constituency with unemployment that high a person is very vulnerable when trying to find another job. It makes it very easy for employers to take advantage of that situation and subject people to unsafe working conditions and other kinds of working conditions on the job site that they would otherwise never put up with. People are very vulnerable. Yet this government goes after those unemployed people.
What else does the government go after? It goes after the Crow rate, the historic arrangement between the Government of Canada and the farmers of the prairies which transports our grain to an export position and also for domestic use in eastern Canada under guaranteed
regulatory rates. The government has cut that by 10 per cent in this economic statement.
What does that mean in my constituency? It means $1 million to the farmers in my constituency. Now the government is talking about cutting the family benefits plan and other ongoing cuts, and off-loadings on to the provincial government.
I would like to propose an alternative. I would like to propose that we take one-quarter of that $170 million and try to put one-quarter of the unemployed people in my constituency to work. In other words, we are talking about $40 million of that $170 million which the government is now wasting in my constituency.
Where could that money be spent? First, I would like to suggest it should be spent on the Athabasca Road. This House and Canadians were shocked to learn approximately a year ago that in this day and age there is a tuberculosis epidemic in northern Saskatchewan in the Athabasca region, centred in the communities of Fond du Lac, Black Lake and Wollaston Lake.
Emergency measures have been taken to deal with the situation and health care professionals have done the best they can. However, the underlying problems of poverty, poor housing, lack of opportunity and lack of good nutrition remain. Those problems cannot be solved unless we can get a transportation system into the Athabasca region, where 5,000 people live, that will meet their needs. A transportation system will allow us to bring in food more cheaply and will allow us to bring in building materials so that we can build more houses with the limited funds available. We can open up the Athabasca region to commercial opportunities like tourism and fishing in Lake Athabasca, a lake currently hardly ever fished because it costs more to fly the fish out than fishermen get in return. We need that road.
How much is it going to cost? It is going to cost $35 million. The provincial government is currently negotiating with the federal government to get funding for that road. The provincial government is suggesting that the federal government pick up 75 per cent of the cost of that road based on two arguments. It would replace something like a $2 million cost to the federal government of having the Coast Guard dredge the Athabasca
February 11, 1993

River to get barges on to Lake Athabasca to supply those communities. The government would save that $2 million a year. The vast majority, approximately 80 per cent of the people in the region which would be served by that, are treaty Indian people. The economic benefits which would flow from the development would accrue directly to the federal government.

Second, I would like to mention the whole issue of cleaning up the Gunnar and Laredo mines. I see the Minister of the Environment is diligent today and is at his desk. I was surprised to hear from a reporter yesterday that the Minister of the Environment seems to have dismissed the notion of his department participating in the clean-up of the Gunnar and Laredo mines.
For the benefit of the House and the viewing public I would like to explain that issue a little bit. There has been uranium mining going on in northern Saskatchewan since the late forties and early fifties. In those days the environmental standards that we operated under were much different and much more lax than they are today.
When the Gunnar and Laredo mines were decommissioned in 1964 very little clean-up was done. There were very low standards. It probably is not anybody's fault particularly, but the clean-up was never done. Tailings are getting into the environment through leaching and blowing around in the wind. Some of the old buildings are contaminated. Although the site poses no immediate health hazard it is certainly something we would not tolerate in this day and age.
It has been identified as a major public issue because the premier of Alberta saw fit to make reference to it in some year end remarks and it is now on the public agenda. It is the appropriate time for it to be on the public agenda because while we are discussing this clean-up issue we are also contemplating expansion of the uranium mining industry in my constituency.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is indeed an interesting bill to be debating at a time of record unemployment in this country. There is record despair and a record number of bankruptcies in this country. Record numbers of Canadians are unemployed and on welfare. Record numbers of children are living in poverty. A record number of individuals say that the current government in power, if it ever has the gall to go back to the electorate soon, would receive the biggest trouncing of any elected government in the history of this country.
We are here debating the bill for borrowing authority so the government can further its desires for some of the measures it put in the last budget.
It is an interesting time for Canadians. We are sitting here debating a bill that will allow the government to continue economic policies that have been a travesty to the Canadian public.
In order to put this government's economic agenda in perspective we have to understand what it has done over the last eight years. What has it done since it came into power? Way back in 1984 Brian Mulroney was canvassing across the country. He was promising jobs, jobs, jobs and two chickens in every pot. He said Tory times were going to be good times again. He talked about fundamental tax reform. The Conservatives were going to make sure the tax system was fair because under those dirty old Liberals it was not.
What did the Conservatives do? They created jobs, jobs, jobs all right, but unfortunately they were not in Canada. They created jobs, jobs, jobs in places like Buffalo, Detroit, Toledo, Chicago and every border city in the United States because the free trade deal forced

The clock is ticking but the Conservatives do not want to go to the electorate because they know what is going to happen to them. The Conservatives will probably try to fool the Canadian public with the NAFTA and promises of jobs, jobs, jobs again. This time the Canadian public will not be fooled.
It is important for us to understand what the Conservatives have done with taxation. Since these people came to power in 1984 with a promise of fundamental restructuring of the Canadian economy they have increased taxes in 40 different areas, excluding the GST, to July of last year. That is real fundamental tax reform. It is called: "Take more from those who have the least amount to give".
Since this government came to power the middle income groups have paid $1,500 more on average per family in constant dollars per year. Even those individuals whose incomes are around $10,000 per year are paying more taxes in 1992 than they would have paid in 1984.
The government said it had to come in with this new tax, the GST, because that old awful federal sales tax was unfair, that it was taking too much money and was making Canadian businesses uncompetitive.
Do you know how many times the government has increased it? Let me see. I have a chart here: October 1984, January 1986, April 1986, July 1985, July 1987, January 1988, June 1989, January 1988, May 1985, February 1986, February 1986, January 1988, April 1989, February 1991. That is the number of times by budgetary measures this bunch opposite raised that dirty, awful, old federal sales tax that it had to replace with that wonderful example of genius called the goods and services tax.
The implication from increases in federal sales tax alone from 1984 to the time that government replaced it with the GST was an extra $9 billion in revenue.
In short what we have is a government that from 1984 to 1992 has set about a legislative regime to introduce more tax increases and increase the federal revenues at a greater rate than at any other time in our recent history.
The government was raking the dough in. It was coming in hand over fist. One would have assumed, since Tories are supposed to be such wonderful economic managers, that the deficit would have been dropping like a stone. Au contraire. It did not happen. At the same time as it was raking in record amounts of revenue this bunch opposite was spending like money was going out of style. They are probably the worst fiscal managers we have seen in this century in this country.
They misspent themselves into a doubling of the federal deficit in eight years. They have doubled the federal deficit at a time of record increases in revenue, record tax increases, and have also made a new record for record deficits.
It took them almost two years to admit that we were in a recession. It took them less than two minutes after Statistics Canada came out with the first positive figures to declare the recession dead.
The current Minister of Finance one year ago came into this House and indicated that all was well, recovery was around the comer, not to worry, there was a light at the end of the tunnel, things were going to be wonderful again, just in time for another federal election.
At that time the Minister of Finance had estimated that the federal debt for this current year was going to be about $27 billion or $28 billion. Now we find out that maybe he was wrong again. Just like his predecessor was wrong each and every time he stood in this Chamber, since I arrived here, and gave an economic projection. He is not wrong by a mere $1 billion or $2 billion, or $3 billion, or $4 billion. He is wrong by between $7 billion and $8.5 billion.
The man cannot add. He certainly cannot read, because every economist in the country has been saying the direction this government's economic policies were taking the country would lead to further despair and disaster.

Madam Speaker, I must confess that speaking on the borrowing bill of the government this morning is no great pleasure, despite the fact that it is truly a pleasure to be speaking in the House of Commons.
If this government had come close to living up to the promises it made at the time of the last election we would not be standing here talking about having to borrow money to anywhere near the extent that we are. On the other hand, what if we had taken the advice of the minister of fisheries, if we had heeded his words before the last election? In the city of Regina, the capital of the province of Saskatchewan from which I come, he quite blatantly said that if he were to tell the Canadian public what the Conservatives were going to do once they got elected the Canadian public would not vote for them.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
He certainly lived up to that promise because during the last election they did not tell the Canadian public in any real terms what they were going to do other than create jobs, introduce the free trade agreement with the United States and create prosperity like this country had never known.
The unfortunate and predictable part of the situation is that they have wrought havoc on this country such as we have not seen since the days of the depression of the thirties. It is not any coincidence that it is the same government and the same political philosophy that led us into the last depression.
The fact of the matter is that we have not seen such a tremendous decrease in production in this country since the 1930s. It certainly speaks ill of this government that we must be here today borrowing excessive amounts of money and paying excessive amounts of interest on money being borrowed to cover up the mistakes it has made and to cover up for promises it made. The Canadian public took for granted it was telling the truth when it made those promises and it has not fulfilled them.
There are any number of areas in which we could examine what this government is doing, whether in monetary or social terms, and find it lacking on almost every count. In fact it is lacking on every count.
I do not know how many budgets we have had since I came to the House of Commons in 1988 but every one of them was presented in the most glowing of terms. The Minister of Finance of the day assured us that the budgets being introduced would get the country back on track, that they would get the deficit and the accumulation of the debt of the nation back on track and then decrease them.
In last spring's budget the government miscalculated by a mere $10 billion, and of course we find ourselves talking about borrowing money as a result. The promises have simply not been there. Some of the solutions the government is coming up with to try to save some money are just beyond imagination. Some of the programs it is coming up with are unimaginable in their severity for a civilized country in 1993, in the latter part of the 20th century.
Canada has been a world leader in many of the social programs which we have instituted. We may not have initiated them first but in a lot of cases we certainly were not very far behind in the implementation of those programs, throughout at least the first world as it is sometimes called. I am referring to social programs such as the unemployment insurance and pension plans we have, and labour legislation to some extent, although that falls far short of the OECD countries particularly.
We find ourselves speaking at the present time as a result of the mini budget, Bill C-98, introduced last December. We find ourselves in a situation, and this is the vicious part, in which those people who for whatever reason find themselves unable to continue in a job and quit now find themselves not only having had their unemployment insurance benefits reduced from 60 per cent to 57 per cent but are now disenfranchised and prevented from being able to collect any unemployment insurance at all. I stress, for any reason whatsoever.
The government is implying that there are hordes and hordes of people out there who quit their jobs for the most frivolous reasons, with the sole purpose of collecting unemployment insurance.
The situation is similar with people who are on welfare. The implication from the other side of the House is that because of some of the Draconian measures it has taken in the past people on welfare are also out to cheat the system. The fact is that living on unemployment insurance or welfare is not exactly easy street. It is simply a vicious move on the government's part to insinuate that so many people are going on unemployment insurance because it is easy street. Unfortunately it is feeding fuel to the fire of the prejudices held by the general public.
I would suggest to anyone in this House and anyone watching the proceedings of the House that if they know of anyone who is supposedly cheating on unemployment insurance they ought to report him or her. No one in this House would ever suggest for a moment that anyone who is cheating on unemployment should not suffer some kind of a penalty.
The supposition is that people are out there looking for work, but in this day and age when work is so difficult to find and millions of people are unemployed, the prospects of finding a job are very slim. Nonetheless, that does not excuse anyone from looking for a job.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-98. This very small document sets out the very large figure of $8.2 billion that the government is asking for today.
One really has to ask what has been accomplished by this government since 1984. It is difficult to look anywhere in the Canadian economy today and find a bright spot. There are some dim bulbs, especially on the other side of the House, but there is hardly a bright spot in the Canadian economy. I come from northern Ontario so I

have a particular perspective. It is difficult to describe the economic chaos that exists.
It is discouraging that this government was launched into office in 1984 at the time of the longest sustained growth period in our history. The six-year period from 1984 to the spring of 1990 was the longest sustained growth period since World War II. What did the government do? It totally squandered it.
It talked about balancing the books; deficits continued to rise and the Minister of Finance was never right. In spite of that taxes were increased dramatically every year. There were 31 new taxes during that six or seven year period. It is incredible. It was the longest sustained growth period in history. The Tory government increased taxes dramatically and yet the deficit rang in every year at $27 billion, $28 billion and $30 billion. There was an opportunity to reduce the deficits we suffered from the very strong recession we had in 1981-82 but nothing was accomplished. In fact the deficit today is double what it was when this government took office. It was some $176 million then and is now over $450 billion today.
It really is an incredible time and a very discouraging time for Canadians. That is why this government has languished in the public opinion polls between 12 and 18 per cent during the past two or three years.
Besides increasing taxes on businesses and people- and I have not even come to the GST yet-it has really put an incredible tax on the provincial governments. They in turn have pushed that down to municipal governments.
If we look at what was done with the Established Programs Financing Act since 1985, it is incredible that financial institutions, hospitals and medicare systems in our country even continue to function. The provinces have had to compensate for the reductions. The government began reducing assistance in the 1985 budget. The Established Programs Financing arrangements had previously been a 50/50 arrangement. The government gradually moved away from that toward a system where the increase in cost of health care and education programs due to inflation was reduced by 1 per cent, 2 per cent and then 3 per cent. In other words, if inflation was 5 per cent, the provinces picked up all of that amount. In the first year of the Established Programs Financing the reduction in funds for the 1986-1987 fiscal year was $316 million. By 1992-1993, the current fiscal year, the reduction in funds being transferred to the provinces was $5.9

This did not just happen. It happened because the government brought in a fiscal and monetary policy in 1990 which drove the country into recession. In 1988 we signed a free trade deal with the United States. By 1989-1990 there was a disparity in the prime interest rate of at least 5 per cent or 6 per cent. Historically it has always been 1 per cent or 1.5 per cent.
During 1989 and 1990 we drove the economy into a recession and did not let up for even a year or two after that.
The government had the gall to bring in its statement of constitutional reform but the responsibility of the Bank of Canada was to keep inflation at zero. Nobody had ever heard of such a proposal before but this government decided that its policy was to drive down inflation to a level that drove literally thousands of businesses out of business.
This was at a time when we were entering into a free trade deal with the United States, and our producers, exporters, and our forestry and manufacturing sectors were experiencing a total financial blood-bath. Hundreds of thousands of jobs were lost because of the interest rates, certainly in Ontario and in other provinces as well. Those extremely high interest rates of 14 per cent in the spring of 1990, five or six percentage points above those of the United States, drove the dollar so high that they were simply not able to compete.
We can examine those figures concerning bankruptcies in the province of Ontario. Between 1991 and 1992 there was an increase of 4 per cent, 1,429 more in 1992 than in 1991. That is an increase from 29,989 to 31,418. These businesses were destroyed by the fiscal and monetary policy of this government. It is a tragedy. This bill to give this government another $8 billion of borrowing power should not be approved.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that was one of the government's most interesting speeches so far. It has suggested extending the debate until Question Period, in other words, until 2 p.m. I have no objection. I have no problem with a debate on government bills.
Bill C-98 proposes to authorize expenditures, by way of loan or by the issue and sale of securities of Canada, in an amount or amounts not exceeding a total of eight billion two hundred million dollars. That is a lot of money. One billion means one thousand million dollars. A very substantial amount of money is involved.
Canadians and members who speak in the House on their behalf have the right to ask the government to account for its administration of public funds. Parliament has the right to expect the government to inform the House of Commons and the general public on its financial administration.
Canadians have every reason to be concerned about the government's ability to manage public moneys as they should be managed. During today's debate, many members raised a number of serious questions, including the unemployment problem. Canada now has 1,600,000 unemployed workers. These are people who are actively looking for work, are able to work and want to work, but cannot find jobs.
In Ottawa-Carleton 700 jobs were lost in January 1993, in one month. According to the experts at Statistics Canada, however, the recession is over.
Tell that to the 1.6 million unemployed workers. Tell that to another million Canadians who are living in difficult circumstances after losing any hope of finding a job that pays and are either on welfare or being supported by their families. Tell them the recession is over, that the government is compassionate and that it has an economic recovery plan. That is not what I hear at my riding office.
Government Orders
It is unfortunate to have to say this, but Canadians have lost confidence in a government that, as we have said repeatedly, has outlived its usefulness. It is time the government was replaced and the people were given a chance to decide. It is time Canadians had their say about managing change to make the economy more dynamic. That is what counts: letting Canadians decide and meeting the challenge of more effective and efficient government.

This morning we heard people talk about the GST and its impact on Canadians. In the past while we have come under attack by the Conservatives and sometimes by the NDP over what we would do to replace-

Let us look at the facts first. The Conservatives have raised taxes or imposed new taxes on individuals 38 times since taking power in 1984. That is a fact. The average Canadian family is paying $1,500 more in taxes than it was in 1984.
The GST, the most hated tax in Canadian history, was imposed on Canadians without proper consultation. It was imposed on small business despite its opposition to this tax. It was imposed on the provinces without consultation and over their objections.
The GST destroyed public confidence in the fairness of the tax system. It has expanded the underground economy, and I do not think anybody would deny that. The underground economy is made up of those who work but do not report their earnings or pay taxes. If all Canadians paid the taxes they were supposed to pay our tax load would be diminished.
It has undermined consumer confidence to the extent that people are now not spending. It slowed down the economy. It lengthened and deepened the recession. It was imposed at the wrong time. We in the opposition have difficulty having any confidence in the information that is made available to us. I defy anybody in this House to examine the public accounts of 1991-92 and honestly tell me that he or she understands the very complicated way in which those figures are presented.
This morning in this House the revenue minister said: "We have presented all the facts in a variety of documents". He sure has. Finance has done that and Revenue Canada has done that to the extent that nobody understands exactly what has happened to the $29.5 billion in gross revenue from the GST and the net result of the $15.1 billion or $15.2 billion that remained at the end.
