speechtext:
I want to get to that point because that is exactly what I intend to do for the remaining two or three minutes of my speech. We will clean up the mess that was made for Canadians by the Progressive, God forbid, Conservatives. What nonsense: progressive and conservative. How one can be progressive and conservative at the same time is beyond me.
We will not do what the Conservatives did, which is to railroad a tax, the GST, through Parliament with closure and everything else. The Liberals will implement a replacement in full consultation, and I emphasize that, with individual Canadians, the business community and the provinces.
That is the essence of democracy. People must be heard. People must be asked what they think. We Liberals have been trying to do that. We will ask Canadians to help us, through full consultation, to replace this mess of the GST with a tax that is possibly unlike the existing one but will be understood and accepted by Canadians. We are not pretending like the NDP that it comes down with the snow in the middle of November and disappears. The $15 billion that must be replaced will be replaced. That is true. It is income. The
government needs it. Parliament has to authorize it. It has to come from somewhere and it cannot come from Santa Claus.
There will be a public consultation, which is what we need. In the first session of the new Parliament-the hon. member should stick around, maybe he will be there-members will be asked and will be involved. The NDP are always sanctimoniously saying we should not be taxing people or we should not be spending money. In my province of Ontario the NDP is making a mess of the Ontario economy. I regret to say I have no time for these armchair socialists who know everything yet can deliver nothing.
We have been saying for years that the House of Commons and its parliamentary committees should be actively involved in trying to resolve issues in this place. This is a very important issue called taxation, fiscal measures, or the GST. In the next Parliament members of this House should be sitting down with the people of Canada and coming to grips with this issue. They should do so in consultation with Canadians, the business community and the provinces. I am sure that will be done with the assistance of the experts and with the information that will be available to us. When we come into Parliament we will open the books. They will be transparent to Canadians. They will know where they are. They will know where they are going. We will know exactly what to do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too wish to participate in this debate on Bill C-98, the Borrowing Authority Act, which would allow the Government of Canada to borrow large sums of money.
It is rather ironic that on the veiy day in which this House will give approval to this particular bill information has been made available to the public with regard to the way in which the members opposite have conducted themselves and the finances of this country.
It is interesting to note that in 1984 members opposite campaigned on a theme of fiscal responsibility and balanced budgets. Shall we say they were to be the new team in Ottawa which was to have a balanced budget? They were the ones who were to take fiscal responsibility, as they said, to the Parliament of Canada.
They also said something else. They also criticized opposition parties and others who had a different approach. They shunted them aside and told Canadians
February 11, 1993

that they and they alone had the capability, the knowledge and the political will to address the national debt.
In 1984 that deficit was in the vicinity of $180 billion to $200 billion, as I am sure hon. members opposite would want to attest. Those great protectors, those individuals opposite in the Progressive Conservative Party, said repeatedly across this country in 1984 that they and they alone had the capability, the political will and the knowledge to have a balanced budget and to reduce the deficit.
Today, on February 11, 1993, we know the success the government opposite has been able to achieve. It has taken a $180 billion to $200 billion deficit and has increased it to $450 billion. What a record, what a record of the administration opposite. It was a sham when it said it in 1984 and it is more demonstrable today. It is an even bigger sham on February 11, 1993.
One thing it said was that it would bring a new sense of taxation fairness to the Canadian people. For eight years the Tory administration has put in place over 40 new taxes, one of which is the GST, a tax brought in at the wrong time. Canadians from coast to coast have told them that. The distinguished, elegant Minister of Labour knows very well that the people he is supposed to represent in this Chamber, his constituents and indeed labour organizations across the country, have told him chapter and verse that 40 new taxes, the GST and a $450 billion deficit is not the way to go.
Surely this minister has a responsibility, if not to the labour organizations he represents then to his conscience. His conscience must be nagging at him each and every day as he walks into this Chamber. He knows there is only one way to clear the air, only one democratic way to put these issues to rest for the next four years, and that is for the hon. Minister of Labour and his colleagues to do the honourable thing: to go to the Governor General to call a general election and give the people of Canada an opportunity.
I have had some deliberations and discussions on other matters with the hon. minister opposite. I want to say for the record that he is a most honourable person, perhaps one of the most honourable opposite. Let the hon. minister be the first to call upon his Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues to do the right and honourable thing and call a general election to allow the people of
Government Orders
Canada either to affirm or disapprove of that administration which has been in office for four years and 75 days.
It was not I as opposition House leader who stood in this place in 1984 and said the following words. I will paraphrase them. The quotations are on the record. They were given time and time again by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, the hon. member for Saint-Leonard and my colleagues from Edmonton and Hamilton. It was the right hon. Prime Minister who said that after four years the right and honourable thing to do was to go to the people of Canada.
I say to the Minister of Labour and to the right hon. Prime Minister: "If it was good in 1984 it is certainly good in the fifth year of your mandate. Go to the people and allow the people to decide whether or not your administration has been able to live up to what you stated in 1984 and in subsequent years".
The issues of a general election, tax reform, the proliferation of taxes and the GST concern all Canadians, not just those of us who are in opposition. This very day the leader of the Liberal Party of Canada made a statement in Toronto regarding the fiscal policies of that administration and what we would do if we were given the confidence to run a national government.
We believe it important to have economic growth. We do not have economic growth when the Minister of Labour focuses on the unemployed of this country. I remind the Minister of Labour of what the former right hon. Prime Minister, the member for Yellowhead, said in 1978 when we as the administration brought in changes to unemployment insurance. I ask the Chair and members of the House to compare what he said then to what is going on now.
On December 21, 1978 the then Prime Minister said: "This legislation before us is a terrible abuse of the unemployed, a terrible disservice to Canadians out of work". What is more demonstrable, what is more a disservice to Canadian people than what the Minister of Employment and Immigration is doing to the unemployed?
Our party and our leader have called for fiscal policy commitments. We are committed to fiscal responsibility, unwavering discipline, expenditure control, holding off new programs that do not contribute directly to econom-

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
ic growth and job creation, and reducing the deficit, reducing Canada's debt as a percentage of the GDP.
There might be disposition in the House for me to continue my remarks. I am sure hon. members opposite would agree. It is very clear with regard to federal-provincial fiscal co-operation that monetary policy is a necessity in the Canadian context as we understand it today. We have clearly spelled out our trade policy, unlike the New Democratic Party that heels to one side of the issue regardless of who it may affect or hurt and our views on skills training and small and medium size business. Of course hon. members will hear more about these matters in subsequent speeches as well as through media reports covering the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition.
In conclusion, if members opposite were true to their convictions and the convictions of their Prime Minister they would do the honourable thing and seek out the confidence of the Canadian people by going to the Governor General and calling a national general election.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on the borrowing bill.
As most of the House is aware I come from one of the most dynamic and growing communities in Canada, Surrey North. Since the last federal election 11,000 additional households have been built in Surrey. Right now the new Surrey Centre will become the second town centre on the lower mainland. By the year 2010 Surrey will be bigger than the city of Vancouver.
Part of that development is being done by the Gateway project, a $100 million project involving private developers, union pension plans and a general contractor who works with the unions and private developers to ensure that the jobs are filled by union labour. It is now the biggest integrated development taking place in North America in terms of capital construction involving residential and commercial properties.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: All this good news because of the free trade agreement.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
All this good news because of the vitality of the NDP government and its co-operation with the labour movement in developing jobs in B.C.
It is interesting to see what the federal government is doing in a growing community like this one. Last week we had three examples of that.
First, out of the blue the federal government announced that it would close the immigration office in Surrey, one of the busiest offices on the lower mainland because of our vital ethnic population. Suddenly it decided, in order to prop up the member for Vancouver Centre, to close the Surrey and New Westminster offices and move them to Vancouver, to her riding.
An efficiency study had been done of the offices in Vancouver, Surrey and New Westminster. Lo and behold, Surrey and New Westminster were far more efficient than the Vancouver office. An application could be processed in Surrey in five weeks whereas it took six months to do so in Vancouver. An extension of a visa was done within two days in Surrey and took two weeks in Vancouver. Per man productivity was much higher in those two offices.
It will cost the government $330,000 more for leasehold costs in downtown Vancouver than it is paying in Surrey. The total cost in Surrey and New Westminster was $80,000 so it will cost nearly $250,000 to move those offices downtown to prop up the seat of the Minister of National Defence. The Surrey office is a money-maker. It raised $4 million in application fees last year.
This is one of the things the Tories do in a vitally growing community.
Second, the Tories announced that it would close the main Surrey post office and sorting service, affecting 100 jobs. Lo and behold, they will move them to downtown Vancouver. This is after a year and a half of discussion. The greater Vancouver regional district and the mayor of
February 11, 1993

the city of Vancouver have gone on the official record as being opposed to centralizing jobs in the downtown core. It also goes against the structural engineer's report that says the main post office in Vancouver is unsafe and that there should not be a consolidation.
As a side issue, how did this government which values itself on labour relations inform the employees that their jobs were gone? It sent a letter to my office in Ottawa at seven o'clock in the morning announcing that the Surrey post office was being closed.
At ten o'clock I phoned the local union president to find out what he knew about the details and particularly what would happen to the 100 workers. Were all their jobs going to be transferred downtown? Would there be
a job loss?
What did I find out? The government had not informed the union. It had not informed the employees. How the employees and union found out about this closure was by putting me on the speaker phone. I read the part from the press release that said the government was going to work in co-operation and had been consulting with the union and the employees about this decision.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Pitiful.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It was pitiful. Later that morning, of course, I found out from the regional manager that contrary to what the press release said, all the jobs were not being transferred downtown, that there would be a loss of 20 jobs.
We had this vibrant residential community where the GVRD is saying: Keep the jobs in the community where people live. Keep the jobs where the growth is. What do we have? We have this government, for crass political reasons, trying to prop up the seat of the Minister of National Defence against all the advice and recommendations by transferring jobs downtown.
What was the third blow? There was the announcement that the federal government was not going to increase grants in lieu of taxes. It just so happens that Surrey has a number of very large federal facilities. One is the taxation centre which processes taxes for B.C. and most of western Canada. We have all sorts of federal facilities along the border because of customs and excise.
Government Orders
Traditionally we have had, but are in the process of losing, one of the two big mail sorting services. The grants in lieu of taxes for Surrey amount to nearly $1 million. The tax increase in Surrey that would be expected is about 4.5 per cent this year. Therefore around $45,000 will now have to be raised by local taxpayers through cutting school programs, not proceeding with park development that is so necessary, or by raising residential property taxes.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Off-loading.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
This of course comes on the heels of this government already off-loading a number of things on to the local municipalities, particularly through its withdrawal from the unemployment insurance program and making sure that was being funded by employees and employers.
The cost to the municipality in terms of increases to the school board, the municipality and the hospital is well over $1 million a year. The three largest employers in Surrey are the hospital, the school board and the municipality. They are the ones who have had to pick up the off-loading from the unemployment insurance program.
This is the kind of triple blow this government has laid upon my Surrey, the community that is the growth area. It has absorbed 60 per cent of all residential housing starts in the lower mainland in the last five years. It is being projected as the new centre of the lower mainland. Within 20 years, into the next century, it will be the centre of the lower mainland because of its geographical situation and its population growth.
I want to close with one comment. We have heard a lot from the Liberals about unemployment insurance and they have made some quotes which are quite interesting. When the Tories were criticizing them the Liberals were dropping the unemployment insurance fund by 6 per cent, reducing it from 66 per cent to 60 per cent. Now the Liberals are screaming when the Tories are doing only half of what the Liberals did before. Shame.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I had time to talk at more length because 10 minutes is not very long. Bill C-98 would authorize the government to borrow not exceeding, in the whole, $8.2 billion as may be required for public works and general purposes. A number of points have been made and I would like to reinforce some of them.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
First, the government has raised taxes or imposed new taxes on individual Canadians 38 times since taking office in 1984. The GST is the most hated tax in Canadian history. As the member said, I think it was certainly the major reason I was expelled from your party, Mr. Speaker. I had received phone calls, visits, petitions and letters from, I believe, 7,500 constituents in opposition to the tax. I think I heard from less than 20 constituents speaking in favour of the tax.
Having worked as a tax lawyer and briefly as an economist I was convinced that it was a bad tax, extremely harmful to the small business community. A man down the street from where I live in Mill Woods tells me that he still spends two hours a day at his convenience store trying to fill out the forms and keep the GST and his credits straight. That tax is an abomination for the small business community which we know has been creating up to 80 per cent of the new jobs and can create many, many more once a new government can turn the economy around.
The GST was imposed on Canadians without proper consultation and very little was said about it during the 1988 election campaign by the then Minister of Finance. It was imposed on small businesses despite their objections and was imposed on the provinces over their objections.
The GST destroyed public confidence in the fairness of our entire tax system. It expanded the underground economy. I am told by a resident of your city, Mr. Speaker, that an increasing number of Calgarians who can afford it and can have their finances adjusted to do it are living through their companies in order to avoid paying the GST. If they buy a car in the name of then-company, because of the credits and so on a number of Calgarians are avoiding the GST.
That is the kind of abuse this kind of a tax creates. It is undermining consumer confidence, lengthening and deepening the most serious recession we have had since the Great Depression of the 1930s. It is complex and costly for small business to administer and it takes an army of about 4,000 who were hired to administer the GST. It has made federal-provincial fiscal relations much more difficult.
If this party on this side of the House is called upon by the Canadian people to form a government we will have to try to clean up this mess. Unlike those opposite who have railroaded the GST through Parliament we intend to implement a replacement in full consultation with Canadians across the country, the business community and the provinces.
Unlike the NDP, which thinks it can cancel the GST and have $15 billion fall from the sky, our party acknowledges that the only responsible course is to replace the revenue brought in by the GST.
In the first session of the new Parliament this party, if called upon to form a government, will mandate the all-party Commons finance committee to consult Canadians and provincial governments on all options to the current GST and to report within 12 months. Our object is clear: to replace the GST in a way that generates equivalent revenues is fairer to consumers, is easier for small business to administer and promotes federal-provincial co-operation.
One example is the state of Washington. It has a sales tax. I am told that if people are subject to that tax, if they are manufacturers or otherwise caught by it, once a year they write a cheque for 1.5 per cent of their gross sales. Because it does not have the credit system and all the administrative headaches, that tax produces virtually as much revenue as our tax does with its credit system.
This brings me to page 2.28 of the Public Accounts of Canada. At the bottom of that page signed by the Auditor General of Canada there is a statement I think Canadians will find of considerable interest. It is called: "The Debt Servicing and Reduction Account, Statement of Transactions for the year ended March 31, 1992, in thousands of dollars". It says: "Goods and services tax gross revenue: $28.76 billion, more or less. Goods and services tax refunds and rebates: $11,329 billion, more or less. Goods and services tax quarterly tax credits: $2.2 billion".
Plainly, the system is not working. I was not at the public accounts committee meeting but I gather that even professionals of the Government of Canada went to great pains trying to explain this particular table I have been referring to.

In the time available let me speak on what we are going to have to do as a new government in trying to make some order out of the finances of the Government of Canada. Before I do so I will quote from one paragraph of a speech given by the Auditor General in Quebec City on January 19, 1993. He said:

You may have read the result of a Gallup poll in the press about two weeks ago. In that survey, Canadians were asked what percentage of their taxes the federal government wasted. I am sorry to tell you that for all of Canada, people believed that 47 cents of every dollar was wasted.

In other words, it would appear that for Canada as a whole half of the money raised by the federal government is perceived to be wasted by the federal government.
I did a poll in my riding, Mr. Speaker, and I suspect it is no different in yours. The question was: "Does the federal government use your money in a responsible way?" Ninety-seven per cent of those who replied, the highest consensus I have ever had on any issue in a questionnaire, thought that the federal government did not use public money in an efficient way.
Very few Canadians have to be told that the most urgent task of any new national government, I hope the Chretien government, is creating and maintaining jobs and training and retraining people of all ages.
Far too many families with jobs today fear that a family member could lose a job. That is why speeding up the delivery of training and retraining programs is a key feature of my party's emergency economic plan.
Key elements in it include our proposal for a federal-provincial shared-cost program on infrastructure, roads and that sort of thing and an increased capital cost allowance for new plants and equipment. These are to come from existing spending allocations within the federal spending total.
On January 27 the leader of this party said that the people will come first to his government. One of his first points was that we must: "raise the level of knowledge and skill of the vast majority of our students so that we can compete effectively in the economy of the future". He reminded listeners that the apprenticeship programs in Germany graduate 600,000 people yearly, whereas Canada as a whole now produces only 24,000 apprentices
Government Orders
yearly. Canada needs 200,000 to do as well as Germany in this area.
The leader of our party also noted that the role of government must change. Times change. He zeroed in on fiscal responsibility and sound economic management. He committed himself to reduce the ongoing yearly deficits both in absolute terms and as a percentage of GDP, partly by fostering economic growth and partly by "unwavering discipline in controlling expenditures". Quite properly, the $4.4 billion the Tories have proposed to buy 50 submarine-chasing helicopters will not survive the election of a Liberal government.
If we spent the same huge amount on education or training, for example, it would create up to 75 times as many jobs. Until the deficit is significantly reduced other new programs, other than those directly related to economic grants and jobs, must be financed from the allocation of existing spending.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to continue on from where my hon. colleague left off. He is quite right when he talks about the need to emphasize education and training. That has been one of the abysmal failures of the present government.
We are talking about an $8 million borrowing bill today in addition to what the government has already spent. The fiscal policy and the monetary policy of this government has helped to create the recession in this country.
What is the effect of the recession that we have just come out of? The effect of the recession is to weaken the economy of central Canada. When the economy of central Canada is weakened there is a multiple effect on the extremities of the country because the transfer payments to Atlantic Canada, for example, rely on spending across the country and on the health of the economy of central Canada.
As a result of the economic collapse or near collapse of central Canada transfer payments to the extremities of this country and to the Atlantic provinces have been reduced.
In addition to the reduction in those transfer payments the government has also reduced or frozen, which is the same thing, Established Programs Financing. In this country Established Programs Financing is what pays for post-secondary education and health. There is less money going to my province in transfer payments as a result of the recession and there is less money from Established Programs Financing, which means that all

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
post-secondary education in my province has less money to work with.
What does that mean? It means that tuition fees have increased. It means that fewer people are able to afford to go to university and post-secondary institutions. It means that the institutions in my province, and I suspect across the country or at least in many parts of the country, are starting to become institutions for the rich, for those people who can afford to go.
In addition to the increased tuition and the lack of accessibility for students across the country let us not forget that those who are affected most at a time such as this are young people in the following categories: Women, who need education the most to gain equality; native people, who need special attention and special help and are doubly affected; and disabled people. All of those categories of people who need extra attention are doubly disadvantaged by the programs and policies of this government which gave rise to the recession.
At the same time as young people have been affected workers have been affected. This government has paid lip service to training. In each of the last two budgets $100 million has been cut from the training programs available from the Department of Employment and Immigration.
The government has said that the unemployment insurance fund is supposed to take up the slack and it made changes to the unemployment insurance fund. However that has not happened. There has been a reduction in the amount of training dollars from the Department of Employment and Immigration but at the same time the slack has not taken been up by the unemployment insurance fund.
Workers in this country have less to work with at a time when they need it most because there is a direct connection between productivity and training. There is a direct connection between being competitive and having an educated work force. This is a knowledge economy. This is a time when one does not gain wealth through simple machinery, the physical work of one's hands and physical labour. One gains wealth today through knowledge. If we are going to be competitive as a country we must have a trained work force. That is essential.
We have heard every responsible leader in the world, from the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Great Britain to the leaders of Japan and Germany, all talk about education being number one.
George Bush wanted to be the education president. Whether or not he was is immaterial. The point is that everybody has recognized that this is paramount. Yet at this time this government has seen fit to cut back on these issues which are of most importance to us.
In this country we have a drop-out rate in secondary school of 30 per cent. There is a 30 per cent drop-out rate across this country. We have an illiteracy rate of something like 25 per cent. In some parts of the country it is more like 40 per cent.
Can we countenance these things at a time when we are in a knowledge economy and we are supposed to have an educated work force? My colleague is quite right in saying that we are asked today to agree to more spending power for a government that has spent wrongly, that has spent money on the wrong things and that has not helped the Canadian people to become competitive.
The second issue I want to talk about is another one to which the government has given lip service. It is infrastructure. Infrastructure must be a public investment. If we are going to be competitive again we must have that infrastructure.
My colleague has talked about the recent speech of my party leader in which he emphasized the importance of training and the importance of infrastructure. We on this side of the House and in this party have a plan to enable that renovation and revitalization of infrastructure across the country.
What is the attitude of the Government of Canada? In the recent budget we heard about a roads program across the country. At first blush it seemed to be a very interesting and very attractive offer. However, the reality is that in my own riding there is a highway that is partly built which would be an excellent investment, the transLabrador highway. It would be equal to the Yukon highway in terms of what that highway has done for the Yukon territory. In Yukon tourism is the number one

industry. It has been able to build its economy, to build that industry in Yukon, but what does it need to do so? It needs infrastructure. What do we need in my area? We need infrastructure.
The Minister of Finance mentioned the trans-Labrador highway and we were all very excited. What happened? What happened was the offer of $10 million over two years. That is not all. That $10 million was to be cost shared by the province in this country which is the least able to pay. The government is asking Newfoundland and Labrador to come up with an equal amount. If that does not happen then the investment does not go ahead.
We are seeing the nickel and diming of infrastructure in this country. We are seeing lip service to an issue which is extremely important to our economy because it is an investment that will pay off. There is a way for the Government of Canada to make use of dollars it already has to build this infrastructure.
We have seen the example in the fixed link to Prince Edward Island. The proposal for the fixed link to Prince Edward Island is that we make creative use of Marine Atlantic subsidies, which are for shipping on the east coast. I am not talking about cutting out Marine Atlantic totally because we will have an ongoing need for certain ferries but we can reduce that increasingly costly service. We should look at that. We should see where else in the Atlantic provinces we can take those subsidies and put them into roads, as is happening with Prince Edward Island.
The theory behind that is that we take increasingly expensive subsidies which we will have to pay over a period of 20 or 30 years and put them into an investment, in this case a surface road link, which makes a great deal more sense and will pay off in the long run. That is the kind of thinking that we need from the government.
What have we seen? We have seen nickel and diming. We have seen $10 million over two years cost shared 50/50 with a province that cannot afford to pay and has been impacted by the recession brought on to a great degree by the timing of the government in introducing the GST and other measures.
If I were to support and ask my own people to support a government that wants to borrow another $8 billion I would be laughed out of town if I were to go back. They would say to me: "What have we seen?"

What have young people in my area seen in the spending policies of this government? What have construction companies seen in the spending policies of this government? What have tourist operators and fish camp operators seen in the spending policies of this government? We have not seen the kind of policy that we need to improve our position.
Nobody in the Atlantic, in spite of the failure of the fishery, wants a handout. There are things that can be done. There are economic possibilities and opportunities. We need a policy that will seize those opportunities and invest the money in the areas from which there can be an economic pay-off. However that is not within the policy of this present government and we on this side of the House will counsel voting against this particular bill.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to participate just briefly today because there are some interesting phenomena to observe. It was said in the last little while that the recession is over. Someone here in Ottawa decided that in a technical sense the recessionary period has ended and we are now moving on to something else.
This is all news to where I live. Where I live the recession continues. General Motors of Canada made its first major announcement of a cutback in its work force in the Oshawa plant. Almost 1,500 workers will be dislocated in some way by the end of March. Housing starts, although a growth area, are not still not what most people would like them to be. In the retail sector there is still not that kind of movement. People are still reluctant to spend, even though during the Christmas period there seemed to be some relief. However, in general economic terms the recession is still with us.
What can governments do to participate in speeding up the recovery period? What can they do that will be sensible and sensitive?
I suppose that we all look to the south where there is a new president trying to introduce some new policies. They do not seem to be in place yet. Initially at least they seem to reflect that the ability of our free trade agreement to protect us from conflicts, or at least to resolve conflicts, seems to have misfired somewhat. In major sectors such as steel we are in a punitive stage again, even though this was not supposed to happen and despite the fact that in a technical sense it was dealt with in a different way than in the free trade agreement. In

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
my part of the country, in southern Ontario, we are still feeling some very negative effects from that recessionary period, from that entry into a free trade agreement with the United States, and from the uncertainty of what a North American free trade agreement will bring.
For us in southern Ontario times are still pretty tough. It is difficult to convince our shopkeepers that the recession is over. It is certainly very difficult to talk to auto workers. Among those who are taking the layoff now are young men and women who have assumed mortgages, have assumed responsibility for educating children, are trying to maintain a family, and thought they had a relatively secure lifestyle but now find that it is all dislocated again.
There is still reasoned apprehension, not doom and gloom. People are worried about their own economic future.
On the good side there seems to be a bit of a resurgence from the private sector and local government. People are saying that they should not look for big handouts from somewhere else but should try to determine what would be a sensible thing to do. Members have talked a little bit about some of them so far today.
In my area there is an airport that needs a little bit of work done. The local municipal government was examining that and trying to decide if there was some assistance available to expedite that process. It was also looking at our harbour. These are our transportation modes. Now is a rational time to try to do something about that. It is important to note that.
Around Ontario one of the things that has impressed me in the last little while is that the Government of Ontario, although it is hard to tell this by reading the Toronto papers, has decided that there are some government initiatives that must be undertaken. Even though in a traditional sense the Government of Ontario, like every other provincial government across Canada, is strapped for cash it is now beginning to proceed with those announcements and is looking at some non-traditional ways to finance them. For example, it is looking to the private sector to participate in the funding of public highways because it is the private sector that, with everyone else, uses them to make a profit. It is looking at
experimenting with the idea of a toll system for highways which we have not used in Ontario for quite some time.
What it comes down to is: If one is faced with the decision of making a major transportation announcement and there is a shortfall of cash is it not a better course of action to try to find a non-traditional way to finance that and to proceed with the actual construction?
I think it is, because we need the transportation links. Sometimes they are subway systems in places like metropolitan Toronto. In some places they are new highways, such as highway 407 running through much of eastern Ontario. Sometimes it is a connecting link like highway 416 from Ottawa to highway 401.
All of these are difficult to do in the traditional way because the government in Ontario lacks the sources of revenue. Like every other government it is in hard times. It should get this kind of accommodation. It has not given up on the task. It has attempted to find different ways of doing this. Maybe it is not the traditional way but it has two little hallmarks that are worth noting.
One is identifying this as a good thing to do. It is not just having our own staff saying that is what ought to be done but listening to the needs of the general public, of the private sector and of local government to try to establish what kinds of expenditures are necessary. What would be the spin-off effects of that? What kind of jobs would be created? What other problems would be resolved, in come cases environmental problems?
Perhaps what I ask governments to do these days is a very unusual thing, but they should start the process of trying to assist in an economic recovery by listening. Listen to those around us who are in a position to identify for us what would be a sensible expenditure of public funds at this time and entertain some non-traditional ways of doing that.
I see this government cutting back in very traditional conservative terms by being punitive to people. It is cutting people off benefits for this, that and the other thing. I wish I could believe this would solve all of Canada's economic problems but I do not believe it will. I do not think the kind of punitive action such as it is promoting under the changes to the unemployment insurance system serves a positive function in our society. I suppose a hot line could be set up to have everybody turn in their neighbours. A few bucks will be
February 11, 1993

saved here and there, but I bet the operation of the hot line will probably take away any cash benefits received.
I would like to see this government and governments across Canada take a more positive stance. I know that education is a long-standing problem in many parts of the country and our educational systems are big institutions. I am happy to see that in many locations around Ontario we are beginning for the first time to understand that these systems cannot operate in splendid isolation. They have to work together. There has to be a sense of co-operation and a sense of need from the community up to determine how the system is run and what those young men and women do after they have gone through a period of learning new skills. If there is no job at the end of that it becomes a rather hollow exercise.
There are some good signs ahead for us but it would be folly to insist that because some bureaucrat in Ottawa has decided that the recessionary period has ended that it actually has. It has not as yet. There will be a need for governments to continue to do things but to do sensible things and to do them with some sensitivity.
One of the greatest follies politics brings about is that some political party thinks it is so bright, so smart that it is the only one in the world that has the right idea about what to do. I do not think any person in our society believes that anymore. They should not because it is simply not true.
The political process as I understand it works well when a great many people are involved in the day-to-day decision-making process. When it decides that it does not have a comer on the market of intelligence and that it can reach out to the rest of our society, listen to what its needs are, listen to what its ideas are and break from traditional ways of doing things then that would be a unique thing for governments across Canada to do.
I am happy to say I see some signs of it occurring in provinces like my own. I encourage it to happen in other provinces across Canada. Most of all, I encourage this government to change its ways. Simply stop and think and listen to the rest of Canada and see what it can do of a positive nature to help the men and women across

Canada who are still feeling the effects of this recessionary period.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad that the parliamentary secretary has come into the Elouse. It is nice to have one member on the Conservative side to listen to the debate. I have always taken the view, even when I was a student of Parliament, that ministers of the Crown ought to be here during a debate on a government bill. I have raised that point frequently in the House, but I am searching in vain to find one.
The fact is that this is an important measure. The government is asking for authority from this House to borrow an additional $8 billion that frankly this House should be very reluctant to allow the government to borrow. It has borrowed far too much at the cost of Canadians already in the eight and a half years it has been in office.
It is time for a change. Canadians want a change and they want a chance to express that change in an election. The government persists in coming to this House with legislation instead of going to the people and allowing them to express their views on the government's maladministration, its destruction of the Government of Canada for the last nine years. It has done a great deal of damage to our government systems, as everyone well knows.
I want to turn and look at the record of fiscal mismanagement that this government is engaged in and of which this bill is the product. I neglected to say that this is the second borrowing bill in this financial year that the government has brought before this House. Normally, just so people listening to this understand, the government comes once a year with a budget and asks for borrowing authority in an amount sufficient to enable it to borrow whatever money it needs to get a balanced budget in the course of the year.
This year, because it was so wrong in its projections in the first budget it has had to come back with a second borrowing bill and ask for an additional $8 billion. That is really quite unsatisfactory. It shows a complete lack of competence on the part of the government, the Minister of Finance and his advisers in the cabinet, particularly his

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
cabinet colleagues, in their organization of the business of both this House and the Government of Canada.
Recently the government issued, as I think it does monthly, The Fiscal Monitor. It revealed some very interesting statistics. Normally when statistics are damaging to the government it presents them in a different way so it does not look so bad. This government is notorious for doing that.
It will normally show, for example, a graph on the deficit. It starts it in 1984 and runs it to 1992 or 1993 as it would be now. It tries to show that really over the years it has been in office things have improved, or it will go back to some earlier date when things were particularly bad in its view and then show the decline since.
The government always picks on a year like 1983, 1984 or 1980. It goes to the previous recession and then shows how much better things are today, or something like that. That is always the aim in the graphs it chooses. It has the option of choosing any date it wants, so it picks up one of these early dates and in effect fudges the graph. Then Canadians think things are better when in fact they are worse.
In this particular issue of The Fiscal Monitor, something slipped through the net because there are a few facts in it that are important and are not really explained to Canadians in any of the government statements. I suspect that somebody is going to get fired for having put this in The Fiscal Monitor after I use it in my speech. I am sony about that, but it is a public document and I think it is worth drawing attention to this. I am sure that the Minister of Finance is going to come down on this group of people like a ton of lead bricks.
The Fiscal Monitor points out that personal income tax revenue from this year over last year for the same period has declined by 3.5 per cent. Given the large number of unemployed people, that is hardly surprising. People are not earning so much so tax revenues are down.
Corporate tax revenues have plunged 16 per cent. Again given the lack of profits because of the Tory-induced recession we are enduring in this country, that is not surprising either. Corporate profits are at some of the lowest levels on record.
Also, we have unemployment insurance contributions. What do you think happened to unemployment insurance contributions? Do you have any idea? They went up. There are fewer people employed generally than there were before. There is a lot of unemployment in Canada.
It will be found in the employment statistics that the numbers are down over the period. In spite of that there is a 16 per cent increase in unemployment insurance payments, that is receipts, income from unemployment insurance premiums. Why is that? It is because of the increases in the rates. This government has jacked up the rates two or three times. They are very significant increases. Now it is proposing to change it so that people who have paid all this money into the unemployment insurance scheme will not be able to collect when they lose their job.
That is what the government is doing. It is in effect hiking the rates. It has an additional 16 per cent year over year increase at the very time when it is proposing to reduce the benefits that will be paid out of this scheme to people who have lost their jobs. Talk about hardhearted. Talk about the wrong time to do it. It could not be worse. Yet the government comes to this House and says it wants more borrowing authority.
Let us look at some of the other figures. The goods and services tax, the tax that was supposed to save us from everything, was well concealed during the election campaign in 1988 and then brought forward with fanfare as the great thing. Of course the government brought it in at the worst possible time. Almost every economist in the country denounced the government for its timing on the thing. It has brought in less money in 1992-93 so far than it did in 1991-92, 4 per cent less. It is not a big difference, but Canadians are not spending. Everybody knows that. Many of them have lost their jobs and so they are not spending money.
Sales and excise taxes and duties have gone up 24.5 per cent. Do you think it might have anything to do with cross-border shopping? Do you think it might have to do with the collection duties at the border as people come back from their shopping trips abroad? One suspects so. There is a 24 per cent increase in sales and excise taxes and duties.
February 11, 1993

Those are rough figures that were contained in the most recent The Fiscal Monitor. Those figures are important for Canadians because they show the way the government approaches people in this country. It has in effect suffered a reduction in corporate taxation and it certainly has not had any significant increase in corporate taxation for many years.
However, it has significantly increased the very regressive and very expensive unemployment insurance premiums. It has brought about a substantial increase in those so that revenues from that source are up very significantly, and at the same time it is proposing to reduce the benefits that are payable presumably so it can earn some kind of profit on the unemployment insurance fund.
This is an unsatisfactory way for the government to operate. We have said so before. Opposition members, as I said the other day in the debate on this bill, are getting tired of having to say it over and over again. The sooner we have an election the sooner we will be able to stop saying it because we will get rid of this group opposite who are doing so much damage to Canadians and to the economy.
I want to turn to the criticism that members opposite have made of our party. They claim with the goods and services tax alternatives we have bandied about that we have not put any firm proposal before Canadians and will not. They say that is unfair and wrong.
Of course, the proposal on the GST that the government discussed during the 1988 election was vague too. It was supposed to be a tax on everything. When Canadians realized there was going to be a tax on food and we criticized and pointed this out to Canadians, the government changed that so that there would be no tax on food.
When it brought the tax in it was not just food that was to be not taxed. It took the GST off basic groceries. Canadians all around this country know that food is taxed. If we go to a restaurant we pay GST on our bill. Every Canadian knows that. A restaurateur certainly knows it because it drives up the cost of the food in the restaurant significantly in relation to the cost of buying the food elsewhere.
The Canadian restaurant industry knows a lot about the GST. Of course restaurateurs face the difficulties of collection. It is collection of the GST that represents one
Government Orders
of the most significant costs to Canadians and to the Canadian economy. It is one of the most inefficient taxes because it does not dovetail with the other sales taxes levied in this country by the provincial governments.
We have the spectacle in Ontario of small businesses having to maintain three sets of books: one for items that are subject to only the GST, one for items that are subject only to provincial sales tax, and one for items that are subject to both taxes. It is inefficient. It is wickedly expensive. Many small businesses have been forced to hire an accountant or some person to keep books for them only because the GST was brought in.
It was the wrong tax at the wrong time and it is still the wrong tax. I am very pleased to say that our party will look at alternatives and will consult with people on alternatives.
I see the hon. parliamentary secretary, the only Conservative in the House, has perked up his ears and is paying attention to this. I invite him to pay very close attention because this is quite important. I want the hon. member to relax because he will enjoy this solution. It will be very good for him. If he manages to get reelected in the coming onslaught then he will be here and perhaps he will get on the proposed committee.
In a new parliament our proposal would be to mandate an all-party House of Commons finance committee to consult Canadians and provincial governments on all options to replace the GST and report within 12 months. Our plan would be to get a new tax that generates equivalent revenues, that is fair to consumers, that is easier to administer for small business, and that promotes federal-provincial co-operation.
Those are the objectives of our tax policy. That is what we will be looking for after the next election.
