subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is rather sorrowful we have to continue debate on Bill C-98 respecting the borrowing authority of this government, because we have lost so many debates on this side of the House against the government. Everybody in the country knows we have a government that is incompetent and unable to govern with policies that benefit the people and do so in a fiscally responsible manner.
When we look back at the economic statement or the mini budget presented in December we see that the government is not only fiscally irresponsible but is bankrupt of ideas on how to help turn around that situation. In the last years of governing the government has more than doubled the national debt. The government said in February 1992 that the deficit was going to be in the order of $25 billion this year and in fact it ended up by announcing that it would be $7 billion more than that.
If we as individual Canadians were not able to budget better than that all of us without exception would be bankrupt. This government has constantly put its emphasis on the cutting of programs in order to deal with the debt and deficit. Cutting the legs out from beneath the people of this country is not going to help to reduce the deficit and the debt of this country; what we need to do is create wealth.
This government in its statement in December, instead of trying to find new ways to generate growth and create wealth by lending some support to municipal infrastructure programs, took the dreadful measure of making further cuts to the unemployment insurance program, thereby making the poorest people pay for the ineptness of this government. Those people who are least able to pay are being asked to pay the burden of this government's wrong-headed policies and ideas.
February 11, 1993

We have had a lot of debate in recent days about the unemployment insurance changes. The economic statement stated that people who quit their jobs without just cause will not be able to receive UI benefits and that these changes to the unemployment insurance program are going to save the government $2.4 billion. Besides being a morally bankrupt policy it is also wrong-headed. There are other ways for the government to save some money. It could have made some changes to unemployment insurance to look after the problems which the Prime Minister raised yesterday concerning people who do take advantage of the system. The bulk of people who are going to be negatively affected by these unemployment insurance changes grieve what the government is about to do. It makes our situation in this country worse.
I have heard from many constituents in my riding of Northumberland who have spoken about this. I have spoken to people who work on commission, people who sell life insurance policies. Many of these people in recent times have found themselves newly employed by insurance companies selling insurance policies and they are paid a commission based on their sales. The companies set specific targets for them. Many of these people were recently unemployed and this is a new form of employment for them. They are learning the ropes. If their companies find that they cannot reach the target, which is very difficult to achieve in recessionary times, then they lose their jobs. These people would not be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. People who have never before in their whole lives had to take advantage of unemployment insurance benefits find themselves ineligible.
As I said, there are things that the government could be doing in the area of unemployment insurance to improve the situation in this country. However the government will not do them and many people have lost confidence in this government. They are convinced that the government is wasteful. I want to quote from a letter from one of my constituents which I received recently. It points out the source of this lack of confidence in the government and the policies it takes. This constituent has recently become unemployed and states that she was taking university courses part time to upgrade her education so that she could get a better job and would no longer be required to ask for unemployment insurance.
Government Orders
She told the unemployment insurance person who was looking after her that she was taking courses on a part time basis, and that to make up for the part-time courses she was taking she was willing to work in the evenings and on weekends. Because her courses cut into her daytime work it was not allowed. Therefore, she was cut off unemployment insurance. She was penalized for being honest with these people.
She says: "First of all, honesty does not pay and second, UIC discriminates against those they will not assist". Then she goes on to talk about her husband who was laid off from his job but was offered employment in northwestern Ontario. He went to the employment office to see if it could provide funds to assist him to get to his job.
He was told that normally there would be assistance but the fund was empty and he would not get anything. If he had gone on UIC benefits for five or six months there were funds for that but no funds to help him travel to a job in northwestern Ontario. However, he was able to borrow funds to travel to this job and work, even though it meant splitting up the family for months at a time. For the Canadian government it means there is one less person collecting UIC benefits. She went on to ask: "Does the system help those who are really willing to work? It appears not". That is just one example.
I get many letters from constituents who have good ideas about how systems can be more helpful, how the government can reduce waste. I believe, as my colleague said in relation to the GST, that this government must do a lot more consulting before it slashes and cuts any more.
I have a lot of concerns about the fact that this government does not do the proactive things to help increase wealth in this country. We have not seen the promised adjustment programs we require. There is some training but each time the government announces training the money is coming out of unemployment insurance funds. After the government's unemployment insurance bill of a few years ago it no longer contributes to the fund. It takes training funds out of the funds that are contributed only by employers and employees.
We need more training. We need more research and development. We need more assistance to adjust in this country. We need to have this government working together with provincial and municipal levels of govern-

ment, with management and labour, to find new solutions and new wealth creation opportunities.
I cannot close my comments on this bill today without mentioning the unconscionable cut to international development assistance. This government has cut over $4 billion in international development assistance since 1988. Our Prime Minister went to Rio, spoke there of how important it is that the north help the south, how important it is for their well-being. He also acknowledges that it has a lot to do with our well-being. Yet he consistently and repeatedly cuts our government's support to underdeveloped and Third World nations. We cannot for the health of our planet continue with these constant cuts.
There are many people in this country who are suffering today from the cuts of this government. We urge the government to reconsider its position, to be more proactive and to come to this House with proposals. Consultation has already taken place and we really do not need more on many issues. We have done a lot. The government has the information it requires. We have made many suggestions and put forward ideas in the House in debate for years now. We urge the government to act on some of those recommendations and bring about programs that will produce wealth in this country, help improve the economy and get people back to work. We cannot urge the government strongly enough to change its approach in governing this country.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to statements by members.

Mr. Speaker, last week I called on the Minister of Veterans Affairs to give a clear and unequivocal commitment regarding the future of her department and its employees, as well as veterans who are served by this department'.
At that time and again today in Charlottetown the minister made a statement assuring the employees and the veterans there would be no program cuts and there would be no staff cuts to the department. I believe this is
encouraging news for Charlottetown, for Hillsborough, for Prince Edward Island and for Canada.
With that in mind I have to ask the minister to do one more thing. In light of the fact that a directive from a Privy Council official indicated a further cut of 10 per cent could be expected in all departments, the government House leader, upon being confronted with this, would not deny that there would be cuts to programs and staff.
Therefore I ask the minister if she will come into the House and make a clear and unequivocal statement in support of Canada's veterans and the employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs who serve them so well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to urge all members of the House and indeed all Canadians to recognize and lend their support to National Bums Awareness Week from February 7 to 13, 1993.
Bum injuries are a leading cause of accidental death in Canada with children, the elderly and disabled Canadians being at the highest risk. Most bum injuries and deaths can be prevented by increased public awareness and education. Bum prevention through education means greater use of smoke detectors, increased home escape planning, teaching children not to try to hide from fire, and training and techniques such as stop, drop and roll'.
Prevention through education will result in many lives being saved and great reductions in suffering.
Finally, I wish to thank the members of the Shrine of North America, including the Canadian chairman, Mr. Don Bumard of Sarnia, Ontario, as well as all fire-fighters across Canada, for their hard work and dedication and for supporting and promoting National Bums Awareness Week.

Mr. Speaker, in this House on February 3 the Prime Minister in response to questions with regard to a plant in Atlantic Canada locking its doors and moving out in the middle of the night made some disparaging comments about that
February 11, 1993

company and the kind of corporate mentality that existed there.
I want to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister another company in Canada that deserves the same kind of commentary from the Prime Minister. I am speaking of Nationair.
Nationair locked out its workers in November 1991 and has refused during that whole period to bargain fairly and faithfully with the workers. It has gone so far as to reject the mediator's recommendations time and time again even though the workers at Nationair are getting less than one-half of what their colleagues at Air Canada or Canadian are getting. At the same time Nationair thumbed its nose at the Minister of Transport who requested the aviation industry in this country to reduce its capacity. Nationair responded by cutting into the already in jeopardy bottom line of Air Canada and Canadian. Six hundred passengers a day were siphoned off Air Canada alone.
On the other hand the government by itself is involved because it has an ongoing contract with Nationair to transport military personnel from Canada to overseas. It has just entered into a contract to supply hangar services to a Nationair subsidiary. Finally, it has seconded a person from Transport Canada to work for the company.
I think it is time the Prime Minister took charge of this file and did something about Nationair.

Mr. Speaker, in a recent letter to his constituents, or rather in his householder paid for with taxpayers' money, the NDP member for Skeena said: "The bad news is that the choice will be between the Liberals led by a Quebec leader and the Conservatives also led by a Quebec leader".
How can the New Democratic Party endorse such remarks and how can the member for Chambly remain silent in the face of these remarks by his colleague from Skeena?
The member for Skeena has made clearly unacceptable remarks. Quebec is one of the cultural and social treasures of this country, but the New Democratic Party does not seem to recognize that fact.
We do have a Prime Minister who hails from Quebec-and we are proud of that-and is working hard for the well-being of all Canadians.
The hon. member for Skeena should make a public retraction.
* *

Mr. Speaker, as North America celebrates Black History Month this February it is a special time not just for the black community but for all North Americans.
As a Montrealer I am proud that the celebrations started here, highlighting the black community's notable contributions to Montreal life and to the wonderful tapestry of Canada's diversity.
Who among us would not benefit from understanding the role of black Canadians in every facet of Canadian life in science, music, dance, business, labour and athletics through events such as seminars on Olivier Lejeune, a Metis interpreter and the first known black to have been brought to New France in 1628.
It is important too that children are being involved through writing contests for this special month to help everyone understand the multicultural nature of Canada.
Given the strife and racial conflict today, we hope Black History Month fosters through knowledge mutual respect regardless of race, religion, gender or language.
What better foundations are there than awareness and understanding to build the sturdy bridges that will bond the diversity within our society and help eradicate systemic discrimination for a tomorrow of fairness and equality for all.
I ask for unanimous consent of the House to table the Op-Ed page of today's Citizen which highlights "Some facts about black history in Canada" and that this text be

February 11, 1993
appended to today's Hansard as a wonderful learning tool for everyone.

Mr. Speaker, over the past two decades education has played a crucial role in reducing tobacco use and impaired driving.
Much of the success was due to concerted efforts by government, the media, police forces and our schools. Today, in order to combat the serious harm of drug use and trafficking such as death by overdose or even murder, violence, lawlessness like break and enter and prostitution and the economic costs for society, a similar thrust has been initiated through Canada's drug strategy.
Canada's drug strategy works in part with law enforcement and the courts to battle the drug trade. It is through education that demand for drugs will be reduced. With no demand dealers will go broke.
Canada's drug strategy is everyone's concern and everyone's business. All Canadians from parents and teachers to community workers and police working together are needed to make this strategy work.
I urge the government to increase its efforts and heighten Canada's awareness to eliminate the scourge of drugs.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today our Liberal leader has outlined the Liberal Party's approach to economic growth in the 1990s. Here are some of the highlights.
A Liberal government will shift the focus from a shrinking economy to a growing economy. This means jobs with a future and industries with a future. A Liberal government will focus on fiscal responsibility and call for unwavering discipline in expenditure control.
A Liberal government will take a balanced approach to inflation and growth. A Liberal government will promote federal-provincial fiscal co-operation. The Toiy or Conservative practice of off-loading the federal debt to the
provinces can no longer continue. Debt is debt to all Canadians.
A Liberal government will focus on making Canada's work force second to none. A Liberal government will challenge Canada's major banks to give small business a break. We will develop concrete measures to facilitate the growth of our economy.
We congratulate our leader on a program which will put Canadians first.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely surprised and profoundly disappointed by the remarks the NDP member for Skeena made in a video shown to the energy and environment committee of the New Hampshire Senate. In this video the NDP member urged Americans not to buy electricity produced in Quebec, electricity coming from James Bay Phase II installations because:

"There is blood on that electricity".

Not only does the NDP member for Skeena make assumptions about the outcome of the ongoing environmental assessment of the Great Whale River project but he is joining in the chorus of people who are systematically defaming the evaluation process used in Canada and in Quebec, while everyone agrees that the guidelines applied by the commission on the Great Whale River project are the most thorough and rigorous ever seen not only in Quebec but in the United States as well. Even the International Water Tribunal has recognized the value and reliability of the evaluation process used for the Great Whale River project.
I formally request that the NDP member for Skeena withdraw his remarks on the Quebec workers involved in the Great Whale River project and that steps be taken to ensure that the video in question not be shown again in the United States, or elsewhere for that matter.
February 11, 1993

Mr. Speaker, Conservative members attending the NAFTA committee hearings were outraged that Bob White dared bring to committee 20 unemployed Canadians representing the evidence of Tory economic policies, including the free trade agreement.
Extra security was mobilized to control the threat. One Tory insisted on knowing who paid their way and then tried to recruit them to the new neighbourhood snitch program of the new PC KGB to capture UI cheaters.
Not a single Tory asked Lorraine Wilkinson of Windsor how after 24 years at Champion Sparkplug it felt to see her job and her husband's job at Kelsey-Hayes move to the United States. Not one Tory considered that any of the concerns of the 20 unemployed or the thousands represented by the CLC were worth even slowing down the corporate agenda for gaining cheap labour in Mexico through the NAFTA at the expense of workers in Canada.
The workers were unanimous: NAFTA has to go. The FTA has to go. And the Tories will go.

Mr. Speaker, I want to applaud Canada Post for its announcement on Monday of a new customer service call centre to be established in Fredericton to consolidate its telephone inquiry operations for eastern Canada as a means of improving and expanding postal services to customers.
This will be one of three locations serving all of Canada in these respects and will open in the spring of 1993.
This will be a new state of the art telecommunications centre and is expected to employ over 100 people once all phases are in operation.
This development is an example of the way in which federal privatization policies are working to enhance public services on a competitive cost basis. It is an
investment decision which demonstrates great confidence in New Brunswick and particularly in the people of the Fredericton-York-Sunbury community, and one which I hope that other major telemarketing companies will be emulating in coming months.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives have shown that they are not interested in listening to those who argue that Canada must change its refugee policy.
Perhaps ministers will listen to their former colleague, Miss Flora MacDonald, my predecessor as member of Parliament for Kingston and the Islands. Noting that the government spends about $300 million processing the
50,000	refugees who come here each year while donating only $20 million a year to help those trapped in refugee camps world-wide Miss MacDonald said in a recent interview that she is "appalled by this allocation of resources".
Canadians are also appalled by the government's apparent inability to help those in dire need. While we must assist those refugees who make it to our shores, often jumping the line, we ignore the millions more who are trapped in poverty and famine.
I urge the Minister of Finance to listen to the views expressed by his former cabinet colleague and provide adequate funding to those agencies who help refugees around the globe. We need more bang for the buck in our efforts to assist refugees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians again have been misled and manipulated by the CBC with its blatantly biased accounting of the activities surrounding the wolf hunt in the Yukon.
Anyone knowing the facts of the wolf and wildlife population in Yukon will agree with the decision made and the actions about to be taken by the Yukon government. Leader John Os-Ta-Shek is correct when he describes the planned wolf cull as responsible wildlife management.

February 11, 1993
Oral Questions
Let us not allow green activists or pink CBC journalists to confuse the issue. If a cull of 150 wolves is not undertaken an entire region will be depopulated of caribou, moose, elk and sheep and that is a fact.
The CBC should be fostering understanding of this issue and educating those environmentalists who know little of the wilderness of Yukon.
With its coverage this week I do not know why it chose to highlight the activities of the American greens in Alaska and the potential for confrontation.
Cheap journalism that smacks of irresponsibility provides for no understanding of the natural habitat of this region.
Canadians deserve better of the CBC, better information for the viewership and better coverage for Yukoners who are attempting to deal with a very difficult problem.

Mr. Speaker, the most recent judicial appointment in Manitoba is causing great concern to Manitobans. It has sent off to the Court of Queen's Bench a prominent Conservative, a friend of the Prime Minister, a man out of legal harness for 15 years.
An appointment of this kind does nothing for the good name of the judicial selection committee in Manitoba.
Was the committee given its marching orders? We may never know.
This appointment sends a disturbing signal to the dozens of qualified men and women who are prepared to serve on the bench. Hard work and first-rate qualifications mean nothing if the powers that be play politics.
At last count only three of the 25 positions on the Court of Queen's Bench in Manitoba were filled by women. I am told that 14 women lawyers have applied for judicial positions. It is likely that all have been approved by the selection committee. However, they were ignored in favour of a pal of the Prime Minister, a man who apparently sees the bench as his penultimate resting place and was quoted as saying: "I am a tired kind of guy".
Manitoba deserves better.

Mr. Speaker, the leader of the Liberal Party has failed miserably in his attempts to come up with an alternative to the GST.
The Liberals got a lot of political mileage by initially opposing the goods and services tax, but the Liberals' alternative to the GST is deceptive, expensive and would hurt those most in need.
As reported in The Ottawa Citizen on February 2, 1993, the Liberal Party is considering a hidden sales tax to replace the highly visible GST. There are a number of problems with this option proposed by the Liberals. The major problem is that basic groceries would be taxed. This would hurt those Canadians most in need.
Also the Grit sneaky tax, or GST, would be hidden. Consumers would not know how much tax they were paying each time they made a purchase, thereby making it easier to raise that tax when required.
They are not going to tell us too much now about the GST, the Grit sneaky tax. They want to get elected first.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of employment.
The minister thinks he is the top cop of UIPD. He wants to set up a 1-800 ratfink line for anonymous accusers. The minister must know that the idea of anonymous accusers went out with the disappearance of the KGB.
Why is the government pursuing a deliberate policy of portraying unemployed Canadians as liars and cheats?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there will be no 1-800 snitch line. The suggestion had been made by members and other people but the government is not of the view that
February 11, 1993

it is necessary to have that kind of operation in this country to enforce the provisions of the act.
Canadians are responsible people. They should be encouraged to individually act responsibly, which the vast majority of them do.

Mr. Speaker, we are glad the minister reversed yesterday's policy to create a "1-800-rat-fink" line. The fact remains, however, that for the past few months he has been suggesting across Canada that the unemployed are people who cheat the system and do not want to work.
I would like to ask the minister this: What specific policies does he have in mind to help the unemployed, instead of punishing them with his policies on unemployment insurance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unlike the Liberal Party's policy which prefers to remain oblivious to the tax burden on Canadian workers, this government has frozen employer and employee premiums. We have increased funding for worker training to help these people get back into the labour market. I do believe that the unemployed are best served by a government that protects the integrity of this system.
Only a Liberal would argue that today in 1993, with the current high rate of unemployment, a person who leaves his job voluntarily, without provocation, without just cause, without reasonable grounds, is entitled to benefits. They would ask other workers and employers to pay those benefits. That may be the position of the Liberal Party, but it is not the position of Canadians or this government.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest to the minister, who unfortunately is continuing his vicious attack on unemployed Canadians-
Oh, oh.

I think it is obviously a matter of great concern to the hon. member and members on both sides of the House, but I would ask the hon. member to use appropriate language in putting the question to the minister.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister how in the name of all that is decent could he ever consider a policy which would deny unemployment insurance to those thousands of Canadians who, in the case of 3,000 Dofasco workers, have chosen voluntary retirement to save jobs for their fellow workers? How could he ever consider a proposal to deny those workers benefits?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member may say whatever she wants but the law will be enforced. The law provides that no person in Canada will be denied unemployment insurance benefits if that person has no reasonable alternative but to quit his or her job and that will not change.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials of the minister's department seem to be saying something quite different. In point of fact, with companies that adjust to the market economy, trim their payroll and pay severance to employees it has now been determined by CEIC that these very same employees will be classified as quitters, hence, no unemployment insurance.
Will the minister clarify for the House why this government has chosen to hit these older workers at the very time they are in the greatest need?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member is concerned about the truth. He will know, or maybe he does not, that the Federal Court of Canada has already interpreted the provisions of the act. The act is clear. This Parliament has decided that any person in Canada who quits a job because there are no reasonable alternatives to quitting will be entitled to his or her benefits and that will not change.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the minister that is quite a twist on words. The minister knows full well these severances I am referring to are not voluntary severances. Workers take them because they have no other choice. That is the reality in many parts of this country.
Is it fair for these older workers, the steel workers in Hamilton, miners in Nova Scotia, plant workers in British Columbia, textile workers in Quebec, to be denied benefits when their severance is through no fault of their own?

February 11, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again for the benefit of the member and maybe to enlighten him, I quote: "For the purposes of this section, just cause for voluntarily leaving an employment exists where having regard to all the circumstances the claimant had no reasonable alternative to immediately leaving the employment".
In any situation in Canada where a person has no reasonable alternative but to quit his or her job then that person is protected.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

Every day, hundreds of people lose their jobs across the country. The lucky ones are offered a voluntary loss of employment with severance pay.
The minister just said it was possible for these workers to receive unemployment insurance benefits.
As of April 1 this year the government's proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act would deprive these people of benefits after the severance period. Loss of employment, whether voluntary or not, means just that, and it is hard to take. Why should these people who contributed to the Unemployment Insurance Fund be deprived of what is rightly theirs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the umpteenth time, in Canada a person who leaves his job because he has no reasonable alternative will be protected under the Unemployment Insurance Act, as he is now.
The hon. member rises in the House to claim in front of Canadians that for those who are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits the issue of just cause will be different after April 1, while that is absolutely false. The only difference is that to protect the integrity of the unemployment insurance fund and protect taxpayers across the country the government has decided that anyone who without provocation, without reason, without just cause, leaves a job should not expect other
Canadians to pay his benefits. I think that is a position Canadians support.

Mr. Speaker, the minister continues to attack the unemployed and to say that those people who have a choice to take early severance or early leave will receive benefits. I suggest to him that he would like to talk to the director of public affairs for employment and immigration who has said the opposite. I will leave that with the minister.
Yesterday the minister said that he was welcoming the idea of a hot line or a snitch line for UI cheaters. Today he says he does not. I guess it shows one day makes a big difference.
I hope the minister comes to my office in Whitehorse and takes the hundreds of calls we get weekly from workers who simply want the benefits due to them. They are not fraudulent. They are not cheaters. They are laid-off miners who are suffering, who cannot get their benefits for eight or 10 weeks. Laid-off miners in Faro and Watson Lake, Yukon are still waiting after eight weeks to get their benefits.
If the minister wants to talk on the phone, this is where he-
I would ask the hon. member to put the question.
Will the minister stop attacking the unemployed, start addressing unemployment in this country and make sure that workers get the benefits they are owed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem politically expedient for the hon. member to twist the fact that yesterday at the suggestion of members and others I said I would consider any suggestion. The difference between her members and mine is that we are making suggestions to improve the situation. I do not think she should have a problem with that.
As for the people in her riding or anywhere in Canada,
I want to assure Canadians that the Unemployment Insurance Act will continue to be implemented fairly. If there are ways we can improve the way the act is
February 11, 1993

administered, the intent is not to deprive good hardworking Canadians of the benefits they are entitled to. It is simply a measure to try to protect the taxpayers, the workers and the employers who pay into this account.
All we are saying is that a person who voluntarily without any reason whatsoever wants to quit his or her job should not ask other Canadians to pay the benefits.

Mr. Speaker, the government has said the UI cuts will save $300 million this year. The Auditor General through the Department of National Revenue has said that the government could save $1.2 billion a year by cutting down on income tax fraud.
As the minister wants suggestions, I will give him some. Kill this UI bill that is simply punishing workers. Instead of giving a club to the little guy, why not give him a carrot? Make sure that the unemployed get the benefits due to them. Cut down on tax fraud. Far more money will be saved for the Canadian taxpayers. They are really who the minister is worried about.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I invite the hon. member to read the royal commission report from the province of Newfoundland and Labrador on the UI system.
The hon. member would be well advised to take into account the impact of the Unemployment Insurance Act in certain regions of the country and what it does to our people. This is also about trying to foster self-sufficiency among Canadians and avoiding measures that create dependency.
I know the hon. member for political reasons wants everybody to believe they will be deprived of rights, but I can assure Canadians who have no alternative but to quit their jobs that they will be fully protected under the Unemployment Insurance Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned this morning that between October 1991 and September 1992, 44,539 claims for UI benefits in Quebec were challenged and the claimants were subject to penalties varying from 7 to 12 weeks. If the proposed UI reform had been in effect during that period, these
Oral Questions
44,539 claimants would have had no income in a province where unemployment is about 13 per cent.
Does the minister think that these 44,539 Quebecers are cheaters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we never, and I never, called someone a cheater for voluntarily quitting a job for no reason, quite the contrary. Far be it from me to call that person a cheater for only taking advantage of the provisions of the act.
Right now there is indeed an incentive in the legislation which encourages people to quit their job for no reason. These people rely on other workers and employers to pay them benefits.
All we are saying is that today, given that we must protect the UI fund and the integrity of the system, we can no longer afford to pay benefits to people who, without provocation or reason, quit their job for no just cause. That is all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister keeps referring to the notion of just cause.
That is reality.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport tells me that is reality. Let me ask a real question. With this bill, given that we have an economy in which the number of jobs is always decreasing, if an employee receives severance pay is that just cause to qualify for UI benefits? In his regulations, the minister says that people must first justify their action, and prove that they have used all available means to find another job.
If a company negotiates with its employees to reduce its work force do those employees qualify? That is reality.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will surely be reassured to know that a claimant is justified in quitting his job voluntarily if, given all the circumstances, the only reasonable option was for him to leave immediately.
This is the test which is used by UI officers as well as by the courts in this country. In the circumstances described by the hon. member, if this was the only reasonable solution for that person then that person would qualify.

February 11, 1993
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of employment.
I quote in part a statement which the hon. member for Laval-Est is said to have made concerning the unemployed: "I have reported some myself and I am still alive. I am fed up with paying taxes and giving to the poor. I want everybody to be rich because if I am surrounded by poor people, some day they will steal from me or kill me". Does the minister endorse such comments? Why does this government continue to force upon Canadians policies which turn them against one another? I find this situation-

I have listened with some care to the question and I must say at the moment that I think it is out of order. The hon. member may want to put a question to the minister, but it is not appropriate to ask the minister what he thinks about what somebody else may or may not have said.
Mr. Speaker, my question is very simple. And here is a comment from a parliamentary secretary who says that he supports-
I have asked the hon. member to rephrase his question and I know that he would want to co-operate.
Is that the policy of the minister and his government? Yes or no.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government's policy is to protect the integrity of the unemployment insurance system and to protect Canadian taxpayers by taking action to help our economy recover so that we have much less unemployment. I believe that the economic statement of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, in December was a very big step in that direction.
Mr. Speaker, I have another quotation attributed to the same individual with respect to reporting others.
Order, order.

Members can argue about it later if they wish. At the moment I am not satisfied with the way the question is being put. I am asking the hon. member to put a question directly to the minister and I am not entering into debate as to what somebody said or did not say.

My question then is a very simple one. As a result of an article I have read I am asking the minister why he and his government are putting in place police state-type tactics where Canadians are rewarded for snitching on their neighbours or family members.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously the hon. member wrote his question before the start of Question Period. If he looks at Hansard he will find that I answered that earlier.
Reporting others. Don't you know the difference?
As I indicated earlier, there will be no 1-800 snitch line.
No telephone, but will you permit the reporting of others?
Drop dead.
I don't plan on dropping dead.

I would like to remind hon. members that the public of Canada in elections do not send members here to be faint of heart.
On the other hand it is necessary to conduct our affairs with some kind of civility, or else there will be no freedom of speech at all. I am asking hon. members to co-operate in that regard.

My question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Time and time again the minister has referred to 225,000 abusers in the UI system, manufacturing for political gain a perception of huge numbers of abusers. I ask the minister to table statistics.
How many people gave sexual harassment as a reason for quitting their jobs? How many people had to move with a spouse or care for a child? How many people, like the Nova Scotia dragger crews, gave health and safety as a reason? How many had a just cause for quitting that was rejected by the system?

February 11, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously we do not have the time in Question Period to answer that question.
Thble it.
The Order Paper is the answer to your question.

I listened very carefully to the question. The minister was prepared to rise in response. However I have to point out that if one wanted to analyse the question very strictly, it was a question more designed for the Order Paper as it involved a lot of facts and figures. The hon. member knows perfectly well that ordinarily that is a question to be put in another way than as a verbal question in Question Period.

Mr. Speaker,
I assure the minister that the question will be forthcoming through the Order Paper.
My supplementary question is for the same minister. How does the minister propose to benefit the economy by restricting the local purchasing power of the unemployed through a reduction from 60 per cent to 57 per cent in benefits, taking away about $200,000 per month in the Timmins area alone?
In addition, how will it benefit taxpayers to have their provincial and municipal governments paying out more money in welfare payments as a result of Bill C-105?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of Bill C-105 and the measures the Minister of Finance announced in December, Canadians will actually have to pay less tax than they would have paid prior to the statement of the Minister of Finance.
The argument of the hon. member that people will be left with less spending money in their pockets does not bear up in light of the reductions the minister announced and confirmed in December.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Oral Questions
This minister has repeatedly insisted that it will not be difficult for victims of sexual harassment to receive UI, but his employees have a document stating that a woman who is sexually harassed cannot quit her job and receive UI until she has demanded a transfer, used her collective agreement, hired a lawyer to make application under provincial and federal law, and tried to prove her case under the charter of rights. Even then it might take up to nine months to receive UI.
Why has the minister continued to tell the House that sexually harassed women would have no problem collecting UI when his departmental policy is so clearly the opposite?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that the document to which the hon. member is referring was not government policy.
This is a draft document that has been circulated at some levels in the department. Instructions and directives will be given to employees of the Department of Employment and Immigration to administer these provisions in a fair way so that women will not be deprived of their rights under the act.
I can assure the member that great care will be devoted to ensuring that on this sensitive issue women are protected.

Mr. Speaker, we need more than that kind of assurance. The minister knows that current procedures to attempt to prove just cause in sexual harassment or other matters are a sham.
Rather than just ensure, will the minister outline today what new procedures he has put in place to protect such workers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is very sensitive to this issue of sexual harassment. I have met with my colleague, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. I have also received a lot of assistance from the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration.
We are in a position to assure Canadians that everything will be done to ensure that these women are treated fairly.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Since 1949 the federal government has agreed to pay grants in lieu of taxes to Canadian municipalities for municipal services to federal facilities. Now, suddenly and without consultation the government has changed this system. For example, the city of Montreal will lose $10 million this year, $10 million that the people of Montreal need.
I ask the minister to cancel this freeze immediately and to continue his discussions with the cities.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had studied this subject he would know that it has been a very fast rising cost to the federal government. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications and involves the iniquitous 976 use by Bell Canada and other telephone companies as a money-making scheme.
This number is supplied to anybody who wants to make a deal with Bell and anybody who uses the phone number pays a fee on their telephone bill for the use of the line.

Mr. Speaker, generally I try to avoid stepping in messes but I would be pleased to accept my friend's invitation.
It is not the fault of Bell Canada that individuals or companies take out 1-976 numbers. Indeed the most recent instance was one where people who had received notices from the provincial attorney general's office in Toronto of having unpaid traffic fines received a notice suggesting they should call a 1-976 number only to discover that upon calling it they got a recorded message and were charged $24 for doing it.
I have brought this to the attention of the CRTC whose responsibility it is to protect consumers from scam artists.
I would invite consumers to contact Bell Canada to ask that any unfair charges be dropped because this is provided for in the Bell tariffs.

February 11, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from remarks made by the hon. member for Abitibi.
In the remarks contained in today's La Presse it states: [Translation]
Guy Saint-Julien, Tory MP for Abitibi, struggled to find words to express his disappointment yesterday upon hearing this kind of statement from a Canadian. "I was surprised and deeply disappointed. This is serious, this is a case of intellectual racism directed against Quebec".

The concern that I have is in the utilization of the words "intellectual racism" in relation to a video which I have never seen and is in the hands of people who I do not know. In fact it is in the United States.
The remarks I made at some point in the past in relation to either James Bay I or James Bay II were certainly true at the time they were made. For the member for Quebec Hydro to be making these kinds of allegations outside and inside the House and using the words intellectual racism is quite improper and contravenes my rights and privileges in a free and democratic society and should be withdrawn.

I have a short question and then I will listen to the hon. member for Abitibi.
I want to be absolutely sure about this. The statements to which the hon. member referred were made outside this House. Is that correct?

Mr. Speaker, I am not here to avoid criticism, and I wish to raise a point of order on the same matter.
On February 8, 1993 a video was screened before the New Hampshire Senate Committee on the Environment, in which the NDP member for Skeena was introduced as the MP from the National Democratic Party of Canada. The hon. member said in this video:

"There should not be any question in the mind of any American consumer in buying power from the province of Quebec that comes from the James Bay II project. There is blood on that electricity".

The video was produced by McAusland Film and Video Inc., under No. MA-617-329-7335. In my statement to Lisa Binsse, reporter with La Presse, I said that the hon. member's statement-
Earlier, the NDP member for Skeena said twice that I attacked what he said. I did not attack him as a member from British Columbia. I told the reporter that what the hon. member for Skeena had said was a direct attack against Quebec workers at James Bay and the Government of Canada.
I was once a technical survey worker with Hydro, a job I held from 1965 to 1968. When the NDP member for Skeena says in this video: "There is blood on that electricity", it is a serious matter. It is unfair to the employees of Hydro-Quebec and to the Cree and Inuit of James Bay.
The James Bay Cree and Inuit have always used the courts to defend their rights. There has never been bloodshed. The same applies to Hydro-Quebec workers.
I think it is odd that the hon. member for Skeena should say there is blood on that electricity, in referring to hydro projects in Quebec, while there are hydro dams in British Columbia and the other provinces as well.
It was not my intention to call the hon. member for Skeena a racist. I was mainly concerned about his reference, in a video that was screened for the Americans, to Quebec workers who have been employed by Hydro-Quebec on major dam-building projects for many years and will be in the future as well.

I thank the hon. member for Abitibi for his comments.

I want to say this to the House. First of all, except under very rare and unusual circumstances I have no authority to rule on statements made outside this House.
February 11, 1993

Government Orders

I think we can all have some sympathy with the concern of the hon. member for Skeena if there was an implication that another hon. member was referring to him or to any other member here as racist. The hon. member for Abitibi has made it very clear that was not the intention, even though the comment was made outside the House.
I do want to say this. I think we are at a stage in the history of our country where we should be very careful in our language and what we say about each other, whether it is in the House or outside the House, with respect to any suggestion that anybody is a racist.
We have gone through a very difficult period of time in this country and some things have been said outside this place and by people right across the country that I hope upon reflection a lot of people regret having said and a lot of other people regret having heard. I think it is very important that we carefully watch how we express ourselves out of respect for each other and this country. Again, I thank the hon. member for Abitibi. Strictly speaking procedurally it was not necessary for him to reply but he has done so generously and I think he has added to the dignity of this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to rise this afternoon to say a few words on Bill C-98 which seeks authorization from the House of Commons to borrow approximately $8.2 billion for various public works and other purposes by the Government of Canada.
The subject of borrowing additional sums by the government is of great concern to Canadians, particularly considering the awesome debt this government has accumulated in its eight years in power. Last week, according to the debt clock in Vancouver this debt now stands at $450 billion. This is more than double the debt this government inherited less than eight years ago and pledged to control. It is clear that in eight years it has failed miserably to manage the nation's finances and today it is asking for $8.2 billion more of taxpayers' money to add to the awesome debt it has accumulated.
Today in The Globe and Mail a Japanese investment house was quoted as expressing its grave concern about the fiscal capacity of the Canadian economy that this large debt represents. A further indication of the mismanagement of this government is the fact that since it came to power it has increased the proportion of this debt which has to be financed outside Canada, causing upward pressure on our interest rates, downward pressure on our dollar and affecting our economy in many ways. In fact the Japanese own $50 billion of our debt. That is a serious issue. It is not one that was inherited from the Liberal government. It is also a serious problem for the Canadian economy.
In addition this government has achieved this debacle while adding significantly to the debt which it has off-loaded to the provincial governments. They have also seen a tremendous increase in debt, which is also a burden on the Canadian economy. We need to be very concerned as parliamentarians when the government

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
asks for $8.2 billion more of taxpayers' money to finance unspecified services.
I would like to say a few words on this subject as it concerns my constituency of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. I just returned this morning from two days in my riding where I attended public meetings to deal with the growing crisis in the fishery which has encircled the constituency I represent.
Last night I was in Canso. We were dealing with how this community and the surrounding communities were going to cope with the loss in income which the downturn in the fishery represented. The previous evening I was in Arichat where we discussed the same question. All around Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia that is on peoples' minds.
When they think about the government's fiscal dilemmas my constituents wonder why we are continuously and ever more deeply in debt. The deficits this government continuously mounts up year after year have increased rather than decreased despite the fact it has provoked a recession which is now into its third year and shows no sign of abating, certainly not in eastern Nova Scotia. They wonder where all this money is going.
We have been paying the GST now for two years. Apparently this GST collects over $15 billion per year. Despite the massive new intrusion on the pocket-books of Canadians which the GST represents, the government's debt continues to mount. The Minister of Finance has been way off on his deficit projections.
The people of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso are asking themselves where this money is going. Why does this government feel compelled to continually borrow more and more money and tax us more for projects when we do not see any results? Our economy is still mired in recession. We are still facing an unemployment level which is much too high. While the government is piling debt upon debt it is cutting out the basic lifelines and support services which people in areas of high unemployment need and depend upon to survive.
For example, the fishery is facing a severe downturn in our area. There will be a need for adjustment assistance or some form of plan for compensation to deal with those communities which are going to be left in a severe state as a result of the lack of fish, provoked largely by the mismanagement of the federal government.
The people of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso say they have yet to see a plan announced by the minister of fisheries to deal with this particular problem. They have been told it will come later this year in April, but people are already hurting in eastern Nova Scotia. The people in fishing communities have no unemployment insurance benefits remaining and no jobs. They realize that this year the fishing will be a disaster.
Today during Question Period we talked about the unemployment insurance program and what the Minister of Employment and Immigration is doing by denying unemployment insurance benefits to those who quit their jobs. Our members have tried to dissuade the government from this wrong path. In terms of sexual harassment, people are provoked into leaving their jobs.
It provokes people to leave their work. Now they will be put into more of a trap. The changes that are being contemplated by this government in Bill C-105, the unemployment insurance bill, make no sense from an economic standpoint because they will only decrease the ability of the labour force to adjust smoothly to changes that it has to adjust to in order to get the economy out of the present recession.
Rather than taking these regressive measures the government should be assisting the unemployed to take training programs. It should be using UI and other programs more creatively in order to assist people to get off unemployment and to find full-time work in job opportunities for the future.
In my area one of the problems which is of real concern is in connection with the student loan program. Many young people are being denied the opportunity to take university courses or other courses at trade school and other facilities because there are insufficient moneys available through the student loan program. That is somewhere that this government could help. If it was
February 11, 1993

helping students that way we might not be so concerned about the borrowing demands of this government.
In addition the government is forcing young people in particular, but also those who are on unemployment insurance, to make the choice between staying on unemployment insurance and not taking training or taking some form of training and being denied unemployment insurance because of silly rules that exist in that program. They could easily be removed.
These are the kinds of measures which the government is not taking and which it could be taking to improve the economy, to get us out of this recession that we are in and to prepare Canadians for meaningful jobs in the future.
I just want to mention that in connection with these borrowing demands of the government. The question which is on our minds in Highlands-Canso is where is this money going. A sad situation occurred last week in Port Hawkesbury with the Premium Automotive plant abruptly closing its doors after receiving almost $2 million in government grants, concessions and generous loans. This company callously closed its doors on its workers. It took the occupation of the plant for them to get their severance pay.
Those people are now going to be facing unemployment with no immediate prospects in sight. This happened after the government provided awesome sums to a company that stayed five years and left.
These are the kinds of policies that have to be changed and on which the government has to rearrange its focus. Since it is far too late in its mandate to do so it should go to the people. It should call an election to let a better group of individuals take over and run the government.
