speechtext: The hon. member for Kootenay East. Kootenay West.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you did it again. It is Kootenay West-Revelstoke. There are a lot of similarities between east and west Kootenay but the current member for Kootenay East and I, apart from having shared an equally interrupted record of service in the House, do represent different areas.
In rising to debate the motion of the Minister of Finance for the third reading of Bill C-98, an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1992, I wish to make a few
Government Orders
comments relating first of all to the government's record when it comes to deficits.
I do not know how many times since 1980, with the previous government from 1980 through 1984 and certainly since being back in this House between 1988 and this year, I have heard continuing statements by ministers of finance and continuing budgets that forecast almost exactly the same projections for deficit reduction year after year after year. It puts me in mind of an old quotation from a poem by Frank R. Scott, entitled W.L.M.K.-William Lyon Mackenzie King-in which he said of W.L.M.K: "Always he led us back to where we were before; do nothing by halves that can be done by quarters". In this case and in the continuing record of the government, it seems to be; "Do nothing by quarters that can be done by halves", at least when it comes to increasing the debt of this country and increasing deficits.
To be more exact, if controlling the deficit is the primary goal of the government then it has done a poor job. The projection for the deficit in February 1992 was $27.5 billion. Now the Minister of Finance says he has reduced the deficit to $34.4 billion. Strange, strange math.
The projected deficit for next year is $32.2 billion. In the 1991 budget this same government estimated a deficit for 1993 of $16 billion, less than half of what it actually will be.
All these cuts, all this hurt for those suffering from the recession, and the government has not been able to deal with the deficit. The best way to reduce the deficit must include stimulating the economy and not the government's failed trickle-down policies.
As my colleague the House leader for the New Democratic Party has said, Canadians are sick and fed up with being trickled on and it is time for a change.
One of the reasons for this increasing deficit is not only the failure of the government to manage its accounts in a better way than it has done but, and I hesitate to use the term drunken sailor, somebody has been imbibing much too much in this drunken sailor kind of spending in a number of categories which do not have the support of the majority of the Canadian people. I refer to what it has spent or is about to spend, according to its own statements: some $4.3 billion on the world's most expensive high-tech helicopters, another $40 mil-

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
lion on studies to purchase these same helicopters, $1 billion on an air defence system to protect troops in Europe against Soviet attacks-What troops, what attacks, What Soviets-and $250 million on anti-tank guns. Great, I am sure the UN will be using a lot of anti-tank guns in Somalia and the other places it is called upon to serve.
This kind of spending just does not make sense in today's world. Eight hundred and twenty million dollars to implement the GST is what it has spent. I just hope that if there is a change of government and the gentleman who is now the Leader of the Opposition, should we have the misfortune, becomes the Prime Minister it will not mean another $820 million to implement a hidden version of the GST. How many times can we get this kind of regurgitation of failures and policy? One billion dollars on an extension of former Prime Minister Trudeau's tax breaks to the super wealthy through family trusts. Those tax breaks were to expire at the beginning of this year, the ones brought in by Mr. Trudeau in I think it was 1973. After 20 years we have decided to extend those tax breaks for the very wealthiest families in this country.
One hundred million dollars in government advertising to advertise free trade, the Tory prosperity initiative, Canada 125, the goods and services tax again, and a lot of "feel good" ads. And another one million dollars on new cars for cabinet and senior bureaucrats.
These are some of the things this government in making its so-called hard choices has determined to be worth while spending Canadian dollars on. It is one of the reasons why its deficits are continually out of control. It ill behoves it to keep preaching to those of us in the opposition-and that includes both the Official Opposition and ourselves-about our alleged failure, according to it, not to come up with suitable alternatives when it is handing money out hand over fist toward goals and projects that do not have support and do not make any sense.
I suggest it start to get its own managerial house in order. One of the other problems is that while this has been going on we have been spending this kind of money on projects that do not make sense. The government meanwhile has cut programs like unemployment insurance, hurting the unemployed; like the Crow rate, hurting farmers; like the family benefit program, hurting single parents and other programs that have hurt those who are hurting most in this recession and it still cannot get the deficit down.
I would like in the few minutes available to me to register some comments from some of my constituents who have either personal or representative knowledge of some of the impacts that these cuts have had on a number of vital programs.
On January 22 Luanne Bush of Castlegar called my constituency office to complain about how the new child tax benefit reform is working against her family. Her husband was disabled in the past few years and so they are on a limited income of $1,100 a month. Naturally they had to sell some property just to get by and that was added to their family income for 1991. They get no child tax benefit for the first six months of 1993. She feels, and I agree, that it is unfair to penalize people on limited incomes who are forced to sell property just to survive compared to ones who sell property just to flip it and make more money.
There is a difference and our system ought to recognize those differences.
Another copy of a letter that was sent by a constituent, Mrs. Val Leslie, formerly of Slocan, now of Castlegar, to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance says: "I hope you will take a look and give serious thought to all the letters you both will be receiving since the budget statement. I suggest: 1. making all businesses pay then-share of taxes, not just some, and the rest get out of paying like some big companies are now. You set the rules that all the working people have to pay. Well, why not eveiybody, including you?"
She goes on: "It was bad enough that you and your government wasted all that money on a useless constitution but it is appalling to see the idea you have now that when a person goes to work and works for years, pays UI to the government, and loses his job or quits you take his money and keep it. That is downright robbery. Part of that money is his on loan to you, to use until he needs it so you have no right to keep it. Therefore I strongly suggest you change the rules you have made before somebody takes you to court for keeping money that is rightfully theirs". She has a bit of a wild hope there.
February 11, 1993

Finally there is a letter from which I will quote briefly from the Employee Resource Centre in Trail, B.C. It represents a lot of people who have been unemployed from the Cominco lead-zinc smelter over the past few years as it has modernized, as all of us have been urging industry to do. This year because of some particular situations in the international market it is having some large scale layoffs affecting thousands of workers in Trail in my riding and in Kimberley in the riding of Kootenay East that are going to have serious effects.
The gentleman who is co-ordinator of the Employee Resource Centre in Trail lists many of the problems including suicides that have taken place in that city because of the inadequacy of the training arrangements that have been made through the unemployment insurance system and many others.
There are many choices this government has to make in order to get the financial management of the country under control and to create jobs for Canadians. NAFTA is not one of the ways to go. The free trade agreement and the consequences of that should have shown that to be the case.
There are many other areas in which this government could move to make things better for Canadians and keep its own financial house in order. I hope it starts listening and acts upon those suggestions.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since you indicated to me that I should do my very best to be extremely parliamentary I shall, and I shall resist the temptation to talk about the Governments of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia in so far as their electoral promises and what they have actually done with regard to controlling the deficit, the debt, services to education and health. I am referring to the cutbacks they have actually undertaken.
I should alert my colleagues to the left in true parliamentary fashion that if they persist in being unfair and insensitive to my party that I have already gathered plenty of information for at least a two-hour address on all the sins their respective provincial governments have committed, that is, the discrepancies between what was promised and what they have actually done. They have been warned.
Let us talk about this bill. What are the issues? The borrowing authority comes up on a regular basis, but
Government Orders
there is a deeper issue. Should the government be going forward? Does it have the moral authority to continue to govern, particularly after four years in government, and especially after the Prime Minister himself has said-of course he was not then in government-that after four years it is traditional, it is customary, it is correct to renew the mandate or change the mandate, to give Canadians an opportunity? Does it have the moral authority? It is really quite questionable. I have support there, the Prime Minister's coach, the then Leader of the Opposition.
My colleague made some statements that I find particularly interesting and I shall follow them up. For example, he said: "How confident should we be that what is being sought right now is an accurate figure?" The government has been quite inaccurate in its predictions. For example, it had hoped and predicted that the deficit would be slightly in excess of $27 billion. In fact I think it is correct to say it is in excess of $34 billion, and that is a large discrepancy. That is $7 billion, which is a huge discrepancy.
The government indicated it would be reducing the debt as well. I have mentioned this in the House and I am always delighted to be able to do so. The former Minister of Finance wrote to me in response to a Question on the Order Paper with regard to what the debt was in 1984. It was $167.8 billion. Of course the members of government are anxious to say that it was in excess of $200 billion. What has happened is really the accumulated interest over time. Of course we know that is not correct.
It needs to be said time and time again that this is not the situation. I want you to note as well, Mr. Speaker, as I know you probably have already, that the government debt has now reached in excess of $450 billion.
Let us remember this. It was not quite $170 billion in 1984. Here we are in 1993, less than a decade later, and the deficit has gone from $170 billion to $450 billion. I would be delighted to show-if I could in this House I would-a chart of the interest rates since that time and to show my hon. colleagues as well as the Canadian public exactly what the figures would be if it was accrued interest only. Now that these numbers have been corrected I hope that government members will not brag about their control.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
By the way, it is also important to say, and I am saying this in the spirit of collegiality, openness and friendliness, that it is inappropriate for the government to pretend it controls its expenditures and brag about it because it has off-loaded them to the provinces so they will have to off-load them to the hospitals, colleges, universities and the municipalities whose own debts have gone up as a result of the off-loading.
It can brag all it wants. It is a little bit like if I were to say to members of my own family: here is my debt; this is what you are going to have to do without. You are going to have to pick up some of mine. Obviously I would be well off. It is the same kind of situation.
It is important for us to ask why we are in this difficult situation. It is true that there have been difficult situations throughout the world. There is no doubt about that. I think most people would acknowledge that. It is also true to say that certain countries have managed much better than we have and it is also true to say that the recessionary policies of this government have led us to a great degree to this particular situation.
It is also accurate to say that when we look at this country of 27 million Canadians with five million people living at the level of poverty or below, more than one-half of whom are women and over a million of whom are young people and children, that these are not appropriate policies. We need to ask ourselves just how much is that costing the Canadian economy in actual dollars and cents and, more important, what is the human cost?
If we look, for example at social assistance, and I am told that this year there will be in excess of 2.3 million Canadians who will be receiving social assistance, what are the costs of that social assistance when those people could be working and contributing to the Canadian economy? They could be feeling better about themselves because they would find some mission in life other than collecting social assistance.
Over two million Canadians will be fed at food banks this year, 40 per cent of whom will be young adults. Some people call them children. It is more appropriate to say adolescents and younger. What is the cost of those food banks? What is the human cost of those people having to
go to those food banks to be nourished adequately? I have not even talked about the 1.6 million and a bit more unemployed. Those are the ones that we know about. How many people have given up?
A recent study showed that every unemployed Canadian costs the Canadian Treasury an average of $15,000 and $7,000 in lost taxes. It is a huge cost.
If my memory is not failing me and I hope that it is not-I am sure that government members would be disappointed if it were-I read somewhere that the UI total bill would be in excess of $20 billion this year. No wonder we have a deficit. No wonder that the deficit adds to the debt, which is in excess of $450 billion now because of those policies.
Today in the House of Commons during Question Period I tried to remind the government as gently as I could that some of the statements being made by members of its party are not conducive to creating a strong, united country where we try to work together, try to build a better nation and reach out and try to help each other. There were some difficulties and not having that statement accepted was disappointing. It was not done with any malice in mind.
It was done to point out that whenever anyone says anything that is hurtful, as was said in those quotations that I would have liked to have entered those comments into the record, it simply pits Canadian against Canadian, region against region, the rich against the poor and does not build unity or community. It simply does not.
Let me complete my remarks by saying without a hint of arrogance, because I do not know what the verdict of Canadians will be, that it is time to call an election. I say this, not because I think it is very likely my party will form the next government but because I believe it is only fair that every four years Canadians should be able to say: Yes, we want these policies to continue or we want a change.

That is what we are talking about when we call for an election. No one is saying this is how Canadians will vote in an election. Canadians are saying: "After eight plus years and after a mandate that has entered its fifth year,
February 11, 1993

it is time for us to go to the polls and determine who it is that we want to govern and with what kinds of policies".
At times I am disappointed. I referred to that briefly when I talked about some hurtful remarks. My leader and the Liberal Party of Canada are going in the direction of trying to create jobs because we feel that people who are working will feel good about themselves and contribute much more than they would otherwise to this country.
I hope that this accentuation of growth in the economy could be applauded by all members from all parties.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-98, which is entitled an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1992.
As one who is interested in words and what they mean I was almost amazed when I saw the wording for this. In thinking that the government would provide additional borrowing authority or that authority would be given to the government to borrow another $8 billion and some more for an overdraft on an account when it thought it would keep its deficit to $27 billion.
Several months through the year the Minister of Finance said: "Oops, I am sorry. We estimated incorrectly and now we are revamping that to $34.4 billion".
If this happened in a private business this simply would not be allowed. When we look at the word "authority", we see that it would be giving power or restoring power upon someone to do that or to have the mandate to do that.
I really believe that thousands of Canadians would agree that the government has lost the authority to govern. It has lost the moral mandate to be in a position to say, trust us, we need several billion dollars more than we thought we needed. I think, Mr. Speaker, you would probably agree with me, being from Alberta, that it is not popular back home.
I do not think it would be any surprise to any members in the Chamber or anybody watching us this afternoon that the overwhelming opinion of Canadians, indeed those in my constituency of Beaver River, would be to tell the government: "We do not want you to borrow
Government Orders
more money until you spend the money that you already receive in a more responsible manner".
I could quote many Canadians who feel this way passionately, perhaps even as passionately as they did in the referendum debate which we all went through last fall. Certainly money was an issue. That came to me several times as I was campaigning on the no side of the campaign. It was so important to be able to say: "Who is financing this thing?"
It was ironic for me, as I was on what in here was the unpopular side of that referendum campaign, the no side, that for every $1 the no side was spending the yes side was spending $300. Many people, rightly or wrongly, saw it all as taxpayers' dollars. Whether they were on the yes or the no side of the campaign they thought they were funding the yes side.
I know it was not all government money that was going to the yes side. Much of it was private money, but everyone in this Chamber knows that unfortunately a lot of public and taxpayers' funds were going to finance that. It left a bad taste in Canadians' mouths.
We need to be really careful we do not go to the Canadian public saying that we need this amount of money. Since 1984 when this government was elected, if we were to look at the budgets in which it was projecting what the annual deficit would be several years down the road, we would see that in the 1984, 1985, 1986 and 1987 budgets the projected deficit, what this government would be going in the hole or overspending every year, was projected in the 1991 or 1991-92 fiscal year to be just a very few billion dollars. In fact I do not have the figures with me, but I think it was supposed to be just under $10 billion.
We are seeing now that those projections, rightly or wrongly, were completely off target. As economic advisers say, they were off because of very many things that went on around the world. For instance, the U.S. recession, nobody was planning on that. It would be easy to say those factors were not taken into account, which happens in the public sector and in the private sector.
I think it would have been far more responsible for the government to come forward at that time and tell us the projections were off and the predictions were incorrect. It could have told us it was in desperate financial straits rather than telling us it was the best manager of money in this country and was the best political party for getting spending under control.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
Granted, this government has perhaps spent less per capita or in absolute dollars or in percentages than the government before it. When we are facing such a crippling interest and debt load we need to spend even less than that. We cannot just break even, Mr. Speaker, as you and I both know, because we are paying 35 cents out of every dollar on interest alone.
When we look at the last budget, as I alluded to earlier, the government said it would be going in hock for $27.7 billion and now it has had to revamp that to $34.4 billion.
In the same vein of interest and debt servicing charges, I am in the middle of an interesting book right now. It is called Bankruptcy 1995. It is written by an American businessman named Harry Figgie Jr.
What I am most amazed and I suspect nervous about in that book is that he is using charts and graphs to explain matters. He has no political axe to grind, he is a businessman. I do not think we are unlike this in Canada but it is on a larger scale in the U.S. because it has such an enormous population. The projections that are given in this book are that the U.S. debt servicing cost will be more than the absolute dollars it takes in in taxes by the year 1995. We know that is very close down the road. It will pay out more in interest on the debt than it will accumulate in taxpayers' dollars. That leaves us with a sinkhole and to ask the question: What will ever become of this if we are not even able to pay the interest on the money that we are borrowing?
It would be easy for us to say that is the United States. It has its own problems and we have similarities but that is the way they do things in the U.S. Unfortunately recent figures indicate that per capita the U.S. debt ratio per person is 2.3 per cent while Canada's debt ratio is 4.8 per cent, roughly double.
We in this Chamber find that frightening. I can just imagine how that feels to Canadians out on the street who realize that their pay cheques are actually getting smaller and smaller. They wonder how they are going to pay their mortgages or buy blue jeans and Reeboks for their kids because they do not have the same amount of real dollars to spend as they did not long ago.
When I hear the government saying that it is cutting spending and that things are in much better shape than they were before I would just make mention of one specific instance. This is an example of where the government says it is saving so much money in costing contracts out for realty service for military members. This ERS service is a private company that is a wholesaling realty for military members as they are moving around within the country and even for those who are coming home now from the bases in Europe. This was touted as a program that was going to save taxpayers' dollars.
I have been in contact regularly with people in my constituency, realtors and non-realtors, who are very nervous about this ERS and the 30 per cent cut that would be delivered as a service fee or charge. This is enough to make a person really wonder about these actual programs that are being targeted to save taxpayers' dollars.
I would like the Minister of National Defence to have a look at this ERS and determine whether it really is a good program, whether it is something that is actually saving taxpayers' dollars or is it something that is perhaps working against what we are trying to accomplish here.
I will close my remarks by making an analogy to those of us who live on credit cards. I am sure every member in this House carries some sort of credit card. It is easy and convenient. However, if I say that my Visa bill is getting too high there is only one way for me to address that and that is to pay off my Visa bill without continuing to go around charging at various stores and putting more and more on my Visa bill. It would be easy for me to say that I can keep spending that money on it, but in order to balance that out I need to quit or cut my spending and my charging and at the same time pay off those bills. That is the only way that debt is ever going to go in the right direction.
I would advise the government to put a clamp on its Visa spending, to cut the government spending and continue to pay off this debt that is crippling us all.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the chance to speak, even if it is only for a
February 11, 1993

few minutes, on behalf of my constituents of Hamilton Mountain on Bill C-98, an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1992.
As the House leader for the Official Opposition, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, so eloquently stated earlier today, during the last election this Conservative government said: "Vote for us. We can manage the economy". If it was so able to manage the economy why was this Conservative Party about the only group in this country that felt it was a good time three years ago to impose a new tax, the GST? We were already in a recession. Canadians were already suffering. This Conservative government had already raised taxes over 30 times.
If the Conservatives were such good economic managers why did they impose such an unfair and badly timed tax: the GST, a tax that is costing three to four times more to collect than the former manufacturers' sales tax.
The GST is a tax that imposes a great deal of paperwork on businesses. It is a tax that has scared the consumer and slowed down purchasing right across Canada and, therefore, put many small businesses and manufacturers out of business. It is a tax that encouraged millions of Canadians to shop across the U.S.-Canada border affecting businesses in Canada. A loss of Canadian purchases meant a loss of jobs.
Obviously, before imposing the tax this Conservative government, which feels it can manage the economy, had not consulted meaningfully with Canadian taxpayers. It also had not taken enough time before imposing the GST to see if it was possible to administer. Therefore, we have had to put up with many changes, many of which have been made to make it easier for bureaucrats to collect this tax.
One could imagine that if this Conservative government could not recognize how much damage the GST was doing to the Canadian economy by listening to individual Canadians than bankruptcy statistics would have wakened it. This does not seem to have been the case.
Let us look at the bankruptcy statistics. Consumer bankruptcies in 1990, 42,782; 1992, 61,822. That is up 44 per cent in two years. Business bankruptcies in 1990, 11,642; 1991, 13,496; and 1992, 14,317. That is up 22 per
Government Orders
cent in two years. Total bankruptcies in 1982, 41,843; 1990, 55,279; 1991, 75,773; 1992, 76,139. That is up 37 per cent in two years.
My constituents in Hamilton Mountain do not happen to think this government knows how to manage the economy; those who have lost their jobs, those who have lost their businesses, those who cannot afford to go to school, those who have been forced to retire early, those who cannot find jobs and those who need to go to soup kitchens tonight to get their dinner.
If this Conservative government still thinks it can manage the economy it should call an election and ask for once, consult for once, the Canadian people. Ask Canadians if they trust this government to lead them during the next four years.
My constituents do not want to give this government the right to borrow up to $8.2 billion. My constituents in Hamilton Mountain and I would guess that most Canadians want this Conservative government to call an election right now.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the moments I have available to me to speak about this request for additional borrowing authority let me say a bit about the deficit and debt situation the government got us into. This is a request to borrow an additional $8.2 billion on behalf of the Government of Canada in addition to the borrowing authority that was granted to the government earlier in this financial year based upon the 1992 budget presented last February 25, almost a year ago now, by the current and then new Minister of Finance.
The fact that it has had to come forward and ask for more money is yet another in a series of failed projections on the part of this government in terms of its ability to forecast its revenues and expenditures for the financial years in advance. I find this chilling because $8 billion is a lot of money. It also comes from a government that from 1984 onward tried to make financial issues, particularly the reduction of the deficit, its credo.
Think back on some of those budgets. Think of May 1985 when the then Minister of Finance and current Minister for International Trade said: "This budget represents a major step toward controlling the growth of the federal debt". That was his first budget.
That in itself was an interesting time. Remember that the election was held in September 1984. In November 1984 the Minister of Finance got up and talked about

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
how the previous government had been spending so badly. In fact he said: "If we do not bring in measures today the deficit by the end of next March will balloon to $34 billion". That is what the minister said in November.
Do you know what? By the end of March he had managed to jack the deficit up to $38 billion. That is $4 billion more than he said it would have been if he had not brought in the restraint measures that he did in November 1984.
What that means is that he spent every nickel, dime and quarter he could find up to the end of the March 31, 1985 fiscal year so that for evermore he could go around saying: "Look at the deficit the Liberals left us". That is completely hypocritical.
In February 1986 he brought in his second budget. What did he say then? "Over the last 18 months, concrete steps have been taken to correct the fiscal imbalance." On it goes to February 1988: "With the fiscal plan presented in this budget, the government sets out a solid five-year fiscal track of significant deficit reduction and debt control". That was before the election. Things got a little soft in election year, people will recall.
In the April 1989 budget, after the election, the Minister of Finance said: "Today we are acting. The government is bringing down a budget that will build for our future and not borrow from it". At that time the net public debt was about $320 billion. Since then, instead of borrowing from our future the minister has borrowed an additional $100 billion, not including the $8 billion he is asking for today.
In February 1990 the former Minister of Finance said: "Within five years the government will begin to buyback its bonds and treasury bills". On February 1991 he said: "We will put government finances firmly on the course to a balanced budget". As I say, last February the minister was still saying things like that. He finds himself today $8 billion short in his requirements for borrowing.
Let me go through some of these numbers because it is very interesting. Take for example the budget deficit for the year that ended in 1992. It came in at $34.6 billion. That was fully $4.1 billion more than had been predicted in the budget. It was just under $8 billion more than had been predicted two years earlier by the Minister of Finance.
Those kinds of projections and predictions have been repeated over and over. In the 1990-91 fiscal year the actual deficit was $30.5 billion. In June 1983, when he wanted to be Prime Minister, do you know what the Prime Minister said it was going to be? He said it would be $3.1 billion. It was only 10 times bigger. I guess maybe that is close enough for Tbry finance.
On it goes. The budget deficit of this year, 1993-94, has had a number of predictions made for it. In April 1989 the government said that the 1994 deficit, the year upcoming, would be $15 billion. In 1990 it said it would be $14 billion. In 1991 it said it would be $16.6 billion. In 1992 it said it would be $22.5 billion. In December in the economic statement, do you know what it said? It said it was going to be $32.6 billion for the current year. They said in December 1992 that the deficit was going to come in at $34.4 billion. What was the budget prediction? It was $27.5 billion.
What did the government say before? In February 1992 it had said that this year's deficit, instead of $34 billion, was going to be $24 billion. What did it say back in the budget of February 1988 for this year? Remember it is coming in at $34.4 billion and the government said it would be $29.5 billion.
What a complete hash of the public finances of Canada has been made by this government. How it can continue to put forward platforms that talk about fiscal restraint, responsibility and meeting its budget targets is beyond me.
Not to say that hypocrisy belongs solely to the governing party. There is a lot of hypocrisy I have heard today in various debates coming from the left as well. When the NDP talks about budget deficits, being from Ontario I can say it knows what it is talking about.
Listen to what the leader of the NDP said on February 8 in Montreal. She was talking about Bill C-91. She said the Liberals in the Senate could have defeated the bill if they wanted to. They could have defeated it "but they chose not to". In fact, listen to these numbers. When the Senate voted on that bill 75 per cent of the Liberal senators were present to vote. When the bill was before the House of Commons-listen to them sing-out of 44 NDP members only 29 bothered to show up and vote. That is exactly what the NDP is all about.
February 11, 1993

I am sorry time has run out because I know my colleagues to the left want to hear more about the NDP record, particularly in Ontario, but we will leave it at that for today.
What is clear is that the problems of the deficit and the debt that are compounding in Canada at the federal level and provincially have to be addressed in a co-operative and clear way before it is too late.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as others have said, it is quite remarkable after this government's record on the economy and the deficit that it would be coming to this House to borrow even more money rather than addressing the concerns of the Canadian economy and addressing the concerns of Canadians to turn this economy around.
Rather than admit errors in the past, admit errors in economic policy, or the lack of economic policy, this government continues on the same track. It is not only satisfied to lose half a million Canadian jobs to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement but is pursuing further free trade agreements with Mexico with the risk of yet further job losses and further businesses going under.
Rather than admit to the errors of the past which have given rise to 1.6 million Canadians on unemployment insurance and over four million Canadians having to rely upon social programs in order to live, this government continues on the same path of increasing the deficit and increasing the debt, rather than bringing Canada's economy into sufficient shape so that we can pay off those debts which were accrued during years of Liberal federal governments and added to by Conservative federal governments.
In contrast, one might look at the Governments of Saskatchewan, 31 years of CCF and NDP governments
Government Orders
with balanced budgets. Not one budget was not balanced in those 31 years of government in Saskatchewan. However, with seven years of Liberal government in the middle with deficits and nine years of Grant Devine's Conservatives with record deficits Saskatchewan was left with the highest per capita debt in the country.
What it proves is that if we have Liberal and Conservative governments we have debts; we have long-term debt and we have deficits. If we have NDP governments faced with a reasonable situation when they start we have the opportunity for balanced budgets.
For the first time in a decade in the province of Saskatchewan the deficit is being brought under control, at great difficulty because of federal off-loading on to the provinces, on which I will comment in a minute.
Of course the problems faced by the government of Premier Rae in Ontario arose initially from the huge debt left by the Liberal government of Premier Peterson. The record is quite clear on that. Any Liberal member who wants to read about it and find out about it can do so.
In Saskatchewan, my province, we are faced with considerable problems arising from the economic policy and the fiscal and monetary policies of the federal government. Times are very tough in the province of Saskatchewan as a result of years of off-loading by the federal government on to the province. The government of Premier Romanow is faced with having to pay off these debts so that we can get the banks and the bonding agencies off our backs and we can take charge of our own province again. Fighting against this Conservative government, fighting against this off-loading, makes this extremely difficult.
We should not forget that the off-loading on to the provinces, the reneging of federal responsibilities toward the provinces, began with the last Liberal government, which in terms of EPF funding made three major cuts to the provinces. Again we see not only Liberal and Conservative governments generating debt and deficit but we also see them at the federal level following the same policy of transferring federal government debt on to the provinces and of reneging on federal responsibilities generally unilaterally, placing a huge burden on the province of Saskatchewan.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
In terms of accumulated cuts in established programs funding by both Liberal and Conservative governments, we see almost $1.2 billion taken away from the moneys which would otherwise have gone to the province of Saskatchewan to provide services to its people. With regard to economic development we see reductions of over $20 million per year from the level of federal government funding.
In terms of agriculture we see off-loading by the federal government on to the province which will require the province to pay an extra $232 million or almost $233 million in 1991-92 and $215 million in 1992-93.
In almost every area of activity which has an impact on the people of Saskatchewan this government and the Liberal government before it transferred enormous burdens totalling billions of dollars. Indeed last year alone the Saskatchewan projected deficit at about $500 million was pretty much equal to the off-loading from the federal government on to the province. But for that off-loading Saskatchewan would have a balanced budget in spite of its huge accumulated debt.
In addition to these very open shifts of responsibility and shifts of burden to the provinces there are others that have added to the burden of the people of Saskatchewan and constituted a reneging of federal government responsibility.
Tbming to the Drug Patent Act which was passed in the Senate recently and to which the former speaker made reference, we note that 38 Conservative members in that other House voted in favour of the drug patent legislation and 31 Liberals voted against it. If all the Liberal senators had been there this bill could have been killed.
The Liberals make a big fuss of fighting the patent drug bill in this House and then when they have the opportunity to defeat it and actually make a decision to benefit Canadians they avoid that responsibility.
The drug patent changes threaten the very existence of the Saskatchewan drug plan, as the finance minister of Saskatchewan has indicated. Again this adds to the burden of the people of Saskatchewan.
Unemployment insurance changes will mean that in
1992-93 an additional $19.4 million will be added to the taxation burdens of Saskatchewan, another loss from the federal government. In terms of law enforcement it is over $1.5 million extra because of changes to RCMP policies. The list goes on and on.
It is remarkable this government would ask to borrow more money when it increased taxes on ordinary Canadians while it provided extra breaks to those who are better off, increased the accumulated debt and cut services. How can the government's financial situation be so bad when taxes have gone up and services have gone down? Yet the debt goes up. How can this be?
In conclusion, the thrust and the impact on Saskatchewan have been disastrous. Clearly the only approach for the government to take is to change its approach to the economy. Instead of being obsessed with inflation, interest rates and so on, it should start thinking about Canadians, those 1.6 million Canadians who do not have jobs, those 1.6 million Canadians who are not able to provide for their families in the way in which anyone would hope to do.
Rather than follow free trade policies which do not work it is time that the government changed and listened to what New Democrat governments and federal New Democrats are talking about, that is to put job creation first to get the economy working.
If we look at the numbers we see that for every unemployed person in Canada the economy suffers to the extent of $55,000. If we put one more person back to work the economy of Canada benefits to that extent. If we put one more person back to work, even in terms of government revenues the government would be $17,500 better off. Yet the concentration has nothing to do with job creation. It is following the big business international corporate agenda of free trade.
It really is time the government put Canadians first, started to create jobs and got this economy moving.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are talking today about borrowing an additional $8.2 billion.
February 11, 1993

Canadians were told that the GST revenues were going toward paying off the debt. Some portions of the debt have been paid off. Today we are talking about reborrowing that money, not benefiting from having paid off some our debt.
Canadians are asking some very legitimate questions. How come we are paying 38 new taxes? How come individual working Canadians are paying more than their share of taxes eight years ago? How come we have the GST which is supposed to generate revenues and fix the fiscal situation in this country? How come we are paying more and getting less? Those are questions Canadians are asking themselves. My colleague from Ottawa South has done an excellent job of demonstrating that there is only one answer to that question and the answer is mismanagement by this government.
The member for Ottawa South documented repeated promises in every budget this government has brought forward since 1985: "We are putting in place tough new fiscal policies; we are charging you more and we are giving you less because we have to bring down the debt and we have to bring down the deficit".
The bill before us today does neither of those things. It adds $8.2 billion to the debt and it adds billions more to the deficit.
After eight years of saying this was the way to bring down the debt and the deficit, one would think that maybe the government would get the message that its plan is not working. It did not work in 1985. It did not work in 1986. It has not worked in any year since, and it is not working now.
Perhaps the government would like to tell us why we now do 25 per cent of our borrowing outside this country. Why are its policies shifting $22 billion in interest paid on that debt out of Canada, out of the Canadian economy, out of where it might do some good by creating jobs and creating economic growth for Canadians? Every day $22 billion is going out of the country because of its borrowing policies.
Not only that, but assuming a 50 per cent tax rate that is $11 billion in taxes Canadians are not collecting because foreign lenders do not pay taxes in Canada on the interest we pay them. Because of the foreign borrowing policies of this government $33 billion are lost to the Canadian economy.
Government Orders
We had a statement in December that was a repeat of the same old promises: "We have to toughen up. We have to tighten up. We have to get tougher on Canadians so that we can bring down the debt and the deficit". After hearing that for eight consecutive years Canadians are not believing it any more. Even the Conference Board of Canada is not believing it.
In its recent report the Conference Board of Canada indicated that the government's economic statement is contradictory: While on the one hand it is in a minor way stimulating the economy and predicting 2 per cent growth in the GDP this year, on the other hand it is freezing wages and cutting UI payments. The Conference Board of Canada says the effect of that is to dampen economic growth.
Two measures alone, the changes in UI payment and the freeze on Public Service wages, will cut projected growth this year by 10 per cent. The Conference Board of Canada goes on to issue another warning. The provinces are squeezed by this government for money, by this government which has opted out of its cost sharing agreement with the provinces. If the provinces have to make up the shortfall by also freezing wages, perhaps even to hospitals and municipalities, it will have a further dampening effect on economic growth.
Does it make sense when this country is trying to pull out of a recession, when the government keeps telling Canadians we are pulling out of a recession, to have the government putting in place measures that are going to make it more difficult to pull out of the recession?
I want to shift for a few minutes to the impact on people. I see that impact on people every Friday when I am in my constituency office meeting with constituents. At least half those meetings are dedicated to people who do not have jobs. Highly educated people who have held highly responsible positions are out of work, have used up all their UI entitlements and are now on welfare. They are trying to keep a family together, trying to keep a home together, or trying to keep the kids in university. In some cases they are trying to keep the kids from dropping out of high school to go to work and support the family. They are desperate. There is despair in this country. There is anger because of the policies of this government.

February 11, 1993
Government Orders
I meet with young people fresh out of school. They have done everything we told them to do. They got educated and trained but they cannot find a job. They see themselves with no future. That is what the policies of this government have done.
I talk to people who all their lives, despite a lack of education, have been able to get one job and if they lost it then get another job. They have survived and they have managed very well. Suddenly toward the end of their working lives they are desperate because they do not see that other job coming. They are asking themselves what they have worked so hard for all their lives. They are asking why they have paid taxes to a country that they thought was the best country in the world and then there is no room for them to work.
We cannot overestimate the demoralizing effect this is having, the way in which it is undermining the very fabric of our society. People see their money being stripped from them because they were wise enough to save for their old age and provide for their own retirement. They see no future for their children.
The middle income families in my riding are despairing because they are seeing their property taxes rise as a direct result of the policies of this government. It has said it will not use the unemployment insurance scheme to take care of people who lose their jobs but will expect the municipalities to do that through the welfare system.
Many of these people who see their property taxes increasing to meet an obligation of this government are themselves unemployed. People sense that something has gone terribly wrong with this country. They want back the belief they had in this country, the belief they had in the future. They want back the confidence that we can keep building a good future for our children. That is what this government has robbed them of.
They know they are not even getting the straight goods. This government says on one hand it is collecting $28 billion in GST and on the other hand it is collecting $29 billion. It cannot account for a billion dollars when people are being overtaxed, when there is no money to invest in science and research, and when commitments made to protect the environment are being broken everyday. One way or another we are taking nearly $30 billion out of the economy through the GST, but how much are we actually getting in revenue? We are getting
$15 billion in revenue. Is that a sensible tax when we collect twice as much as we really need? Where is the other $15 billion going?
These are big amounts we are talking about. Canadians want some accountability and responsibility because they know they cannot trust the promises of this government. It has done exactly the opposite of everything it said it would try to do.
We see small businesses going out of business. The main generators of new jobs in this country are going bankrupt at an alarming rate. We are failing in every way to invest in our future. We are failing to invest in our young people. We are failing to invest in knowledge. We are failing to invest in cleaning up our world.
There is despair in the country and it is a result of the false promises and total lack of performance of this government. It is time for a cleansing. It is time for a change. It is time for some honesty and straight talk with Canadians. It is time for a government that wants to fix the problems.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also appreciate this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-98, an act to provide additional borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1992 and soon to end on March 31, 1993.
For more than eight years I have had the privilege of representing the constituents of the riding of Saint-Leonard in this House. I remember during the election campaign in 1988 when the Conservative Party said clearly that it would put the government's financial house in order, reduce the deficit, reduce the debt and create jobs. All Canadians will remember the slogan: Jobs, jobs, jobs. Today, in the fifth year of this government's second term if we look at what the government has been able to achieve and at our situation as a nation, we see we have more than 1.5 million unemployed, any number of food banks, more than two million people on welfare, and I could go on about the homeless and the rest.
If we look at the Public Accounts, on March 31, 1984 the deficit was around $34 billion. According to the forecasts of the Minister of Finance, not those he gave in the February budget last year but the revised forecasts he gave last fall, on March 31, 1993 we will have a deficit of $34 billion. This comes after an economic recovery, more
February 11, 1993

than 30 tax increases and new taxes and steep fee increases for federal services, including immigration, citizenship and passports. These are all taxes in disguise, and in fact government revenues have increased. Sales of Crown corporations, tax increases and increases in fees for federal services are all increases in revenue.
However, after eight years and some months, we have a deficit that is more or less the same as when they came to power, and we have a debt that has more than doubled. This government has been a complete failure as far as financial administration is concerned. It has also put us in a financial situation that will paralyse us for years to come, because a substantial percentage of our debt is not owed to Canadians but to foreign countries, which will make it very difficult for us to have a Canadian monetary policy.
The hon. member said earlier that it was a matter of people, and I agree that behind the figures I just mentioned are human beings who are affected by the decisions we make here, by everything we do on whatever side of the House we happen to be. In fact, I would like to share my experience of last Sunday. Two government ministers, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Justice, said we were separatists. No one is more of a federalist than the member for Saint-Denis, the member for Westmount, the member for LaSalle-Emard or myself. I do not have to prove that I stand for Canada. I make this aside just to correct some things that were said.
I went there that Sunday because some constituents had asked me to go and I wanted to support them and be there with them, even though the weather was bitter cold. When it is -25C it is quite something to walk from Lafontaine Park to the Guy Favreau Complex at the corner of Jeanne Mance and Rene Levesque Boulevard.
But what did I notice on seeing that crowd? You can challenge the figures but I can tell you that there were a lot of people there. I never saw such a demonstration. We could sense their frustration. It was a cry of alarm because people cannot take it anymore. I am sure that all
Government Orders
members, whether on the government side or in opposition, sense that frustration when we are in our riding offices. We meet people who are on welfare because they have lost their job and no longer qualify for unemployment insurance, so they cannot pay the rent and feed their family and their children. Some people who lose their jobs do not qualify for welfare when their unemployment insurance runs out because they have a small property, like their own house. It is hard when we meet them.
What I noted is that the demonstration was against all this. It was not just against the changes to unemployment insurance. It was against the policies of this government in the past eight years. They have had enough. That was why they were sounding the alarm.
After this demonstration, an editorial writer, Alain Dubuc, well described the feelings behind it. I would like to quote this editorial from La Presse of February 9,1993, entitled "Cry of Anger":
For a long time we had not seen 50,000 people in the streets of Montreal for anything other than a celebration. Those mainly responsible for this feat are not the big labour bodies that organized Sunday's demonstration against Bill C-105 but the Conservative government which handed them this mobilizing issue on a silver platter.
With minor amendments, Brian Mulroney and the minister, Bernard Valcourt, could easily have short-circuited the opposition.
Most Canadians and Quebecers are not opposed to the basic purpose of this law, that the government refuses to pay unemployment benefits to people who choose to quit their job and not to work. The debate is not on that principle, but on the way the bill would be implemented, especially the risk of bureaucratic errors and abuse by employers.
The real mystery is that the federal government did not agree to make these relatively simple changes that would not have affected the underlying logic of the bill. If Mr. Valcourt had been open, he could also have dispelled some fears that are not always founded.
Ottawa's attitude is hard to explain, except that we are already in the period leading up to a federal election. It is quite possible that the Conservatives' intransigence is not a blunder but part of a strategy. Confrontation with the unions and the left that is close to the NDP certainly does not hurt the Conservatives. On the contrary, this polarization helps the Conservatives bring back right-wing voters who had been drawn to the Reform Party.
This would be a sly calculation if the upsurge of anger as seen in Montreal on Sunday concerned only the technicalities of Bill C-105. That is not the case. This indignation is also due to the image of

Government Orders
insensitivity of a government that is zealous in this bill after it made a virtue of not acting to help the unemployed or speed the recovery.
On the contrary, this anger is likely to bring people together, whether they are on the right or on the left, because unemployment and uncertainty affect them regardless of party label.
This editorial reflects pretty well the feelings of those who took part in that demonstration. How many times have we in the opposition and the Leader of the Opposition asked the government to present an infrastructure project? It answers that it cannot act because it lacks the necessary funds. But when it comes to crushing the unemployed we saw the insensitivity of the Minister of Employment and Immigration today. When he was asked how much it cost to hire 100 more investigators in 1992 he replied: "I don't know. It's not important". The important thing for him is that hiring these additional investigators saved the unemployment insurance system $200 million. This $200 million does not have a human face; he did not care about the human side. The government has always neglected to put people first.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, needless to say in standing to oppose Bill C-98, I am standing to oppose the failure of this administration to deal effectively with the major responsibility that it has and that is to deal responsibly with the tax revenues in this country. This bill is an admission of that failure.
This year's deficit is over $7 billion higher than was projected. Next year the deficit is projected to be about $32.6 billion which is twice the amount that was projected last year. If we look at the interest payments alone over the next couple of years we are looking at over $40 billion in interest payments on the debt alone.
That has to be an admission of failure. The government is broke. It is out of money. It has to come back to the House for approval to borrow more money to continue to do its job and do it inadequately.
We are basically being asked to write a rubber cheque. I think the members on this side of the House find that particularly problematic. The fact that the government has to come to the House and extend its borrowing
authority through this bill is an admission of the failure of the last nine years of its administration.
Actually it goes back even more. Let us not blame it all on this government. When it came into power in 1984 it was already dealing with a deficit that was spiralling out of control because of the fiscal mismanagement of its predecessor which was the Liberal government of that time. It had ballooned the deficit to I believe some $179 billion in 1979-80.
Unfortunately, rather than dealing with the deficit and bringing that deficit down to manageable levels, it has taken that debt and more than doubled it from $179 billion to today where we have an accumulated debt of over $400 billion facing Canadians. It is an admission of failure.
I can recall when the Prime Minister was first elected some nine years ago. In his first speech to the House of Commons he made the comment: "Give us 20 years and you will not recognize this country". We have only had nine years and looking around we already do not recognize the Canada we have today compared to the Canada we had before this government came into power.
It has been nine years of fiscal mismanagement, nine years of misdirected priorities, nine years of economic failure. The Canadian people are tired of the misplaced directions this government has led this nation, all the while touting itself as a responsible financial manager.
This is nothing if not a legacy of failure. It has continued to follow the divine rule of supply side management, the trickle down theory, where if we loosen up the tax policies for those at the top echelons of society, the wealthy individuals, the large corporations, if we loosen up the purse strings and allow them to keep more of their revenue by reducing their tax structure then they will be able to blossom economically and the rest of the country will follow along in suit. That is known as the trickle down theory. It has not worked.
I think I speak on behalf of all Canadians when I say that Canadians have been trickled on enough and are tired of the policies of this administration. They are tired of the Reaganomics this government has practised over the past nine years. Look at our neighbours to the south. We have had a change in the political winds. President Clinton has recognized full well that there needs to be a substantial change in the economic policies and priorities
February 11, 1993

of our neighbours to the south. That is why President Bush was kicked out of office. It was because the Americans were tired of that same kind of economic mismanagement.
This is a doomed policy. This government by following the policy is doomed to relegate itself to the dustbin of history. It is proof that we cannot wring out of the economy an economic recovery by strangling the very social programs which provide the safety net for those people during tough times.
The government has targeted our social programs, unemployment insurance and the income assistance programs as being the culprits for the reason it is having such difficulty balancing the books. I want to say that only 6 per cent of our debt load is actually due to the cost of social programs.
When we break down the debt load of this country and analyse where most of the debt has accumulated from we see that over 40 per cent of that debt has resulted from compounded interest. While this government continued to follow a high interest rate policy it was burdening itself with an increasingly higher debt and it had less and less ability to follow.
The remainder of our debt is simply due to the failure of this government to recover the tax revenues that were due and payable to it by its corporate friends across Canada who stuck billions of dollars away in deferred tax payments, through tax loopholes and other schemes such as the billions of dollars that have been hidden away in family trusts. It does not cancel those. It does not close those loopholes. It does not say to the corporate sector of Canada that it is time to pay its fair share.
What government does is burden the unemployed by bringing in Draconian new measures which are going to decrease the insurance that our unemployed Canadians have had as a kind of safety net to get them through these tough times. They are burdening Canada's weakest element, our unemployed Canadians, those who have been out of work for some time by cutting back on the very programs that provide them some degree of security-
It is proof that this kind of policy direction does not work, has not worked and will not work in the future.
Government Orders
The debt problem has been made a lot worse because of the implementation of the free trade agreement back in 1988-89. When that agreement was brought into force overnight we lost over $2.2 billion in tax revenues that should have come to the Crown but no longer did because of the reduced tariffs. That was immediately. Over the years that have followed we have lost billions and billions of dollars in taxes as a result of the reduced tariff structure. Above and beyond that we have lost over
500,000	jobs which directly or indirectly are attributable to the impact and the implementation of the free trade agreement in Canada.
We have had an economic haemorrhaging of tax revenues and an economic haemorrhaging in terms of job losses in this country, which is scandalous to say the least. As well we have hundreds of businesses moving south. Those jobs will not come back to Canada. They are gone. They are gone for good. We are undergoing an economic revolution in this country in terms of the restructuring that is taking place. The jobs that are leaving are leaving for good. They will not be back and we have to find some way of regenerating some sort of economic growth in light of that reality.
We have permanent restructuring going on in this country and the government talks about the need to become competitive. I do not disagree with that. We do need to become competitive. But the policies this administration is trying to implement in order to develop competitiveness in this country are in the wrong direction.
The tools for competitiveness in a knowledge based, information based economy are the tools that are put into the hands of people to generate the skills, and the training, the knowledge, the research and development that is necessary to develop the kind of knowledge-based, information-based infrastructure society needs today to compete with those highly developed communities throughout the Pacific rim and the other countries we are competing with on a global basis.
This government has not recognized that. Instead it continues to cut funding to our provinces, to cut the cost shared programs. It is strangling the economy rather than finding ways of investing in our economy to put people back to work and create the long-lasting knowledge-based jobs that are required if this country is ever

Government Orders
going to be front and centre with a competitive and vibrant structure in our global economy.
This is the wrong direction the government is taking. It is going to suffer when it comes to an election because the people of Canada are no longer willing to put up with the mistaken policies and the mistaken economic direction this government has followed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to use the few minutes that are left to address the questions raised by this bill to extend the borrowing authority of the government and to provide for some $8 billion. As many speakers have indicated, that reflects an increase in the actual deficit for this fiscal year from the $27.5 billion originally estimated to the present estimate of $34.4 billion.
It is interesting to note what is the chief source of this increase in the estimated deficit. It is attributable to an $8 billion decrease in revenue. To what is that attributable? Fundamentally, it is attributable to the fact that we now have 1.5 million people unemployed. It is attributable to the fact that we had 76,000 bankruptcies last year. In my own home town of Windsor, where the unemployment rate is 14 per cent, there is an indication of the damage this government has done to the economy which is ultimately that to which the problem must be attributed.
I want to put emphasis on the fact that in Windsor the unemployment rate among youth is 25 per cent.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Shameful.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1992-93 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

It is 25 per cent. We know that we have been overwhelmed with all kinds of means to save money, mostly consisting of a tax on the unemployed. I just want to take this opportunity to suggest to the government it did not need to attack the unemployed. I say that because of the savings which have been generated in the financial statement, most of which come from changes in UI: $500 million from a decrease in the percentage of wages that will be paid through UI and another $300 million by virtue of the Draconian attack that expresses itself in attempts, for example, to mount the PC KGB.
What the government might have done, just to give a few examples, is to take a look at the meals and entertainment expense deduction, which is worth about
$1 billion. Actually, I think it would be very useful to have spies to count the escorts that are being paid for by our taxpayers through those deductions.
Perhaps it should look at the private family trust tax break which was generated not by the Tories but by the Liberals. By the way, that tax break was among a bunch of tax breaks generated in the 1970s by the previous government to help the rich and help the corporations that are cutting back on those things we need now which contributes to the problems we have. Take a look at that.
How about the tax cheaters? How about the fraudulent taxes? How about the shell game that goes on among multinationals to cheat Canadians out of taxes?
Yes, there is an alternative. The real alternative is the New Democrats and their leader.
